paragraphs.text:
Of our father among the saints [?]: A concise synopsis of the divine Scripture of the Old and New Testaments.

1. All of our Christian Scripture is inspired by God [?]. Its books are not left undefined. They are defined and fixed in a canon. Those of the Old Testament are these. Genesis, which begins: “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.” Exodus, which begins: “These are the names of the sons of Israel who came into Egypt.” Leviticus, which begins: “And he called Moses, and the Lord spoke to him in the tent of witness.” Numbers, which begins: “And the Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tent of witness.”

Joshua son of Nun, which begins: “And it came to pass after the death of [?] the servant of the Lord, that the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, the minister of Moses, saying.” Judges, which begins: “And it came to pass after the death of Joshua that the sons of Israel inquired of the Lord, saying, ‘Who will go up for us against the Canaanites as leader?’” Ruth, which begins: “And it came to pass, when the judges were judging, that there was a famine in the land.” First and Second Kingdoms, counted as one book. The first begins: “There was a man of Armathaim Zophim, from the hill country [?] of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeremeel, son of Eli.” The second begins: “It came to pass after Saul had died, that David returned from striking down Amalek.” Third and Fourth Kingdoms, again counted as one book. The third begins: “And King David was old, advanced in days; and they covered him with garments, but he was not warmed.” The fourth begins: “And Moab rebelled against Israel after Ahab had died.” First and Second Chronicles, counted as one book. The first begins: “Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah.” The second begins: “And Solomon son of David was established in his kingdom, and the Lord his God was with him and magnified him [?]”
First and Second Esdras, counted as one book. The first begins: “And Josiah kept the Passover to his Lord in Jerusalem on the fourteenth day of the month [?]”

The second begins: “And in the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, so that the word from the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians.” The Psalter of David, which contains 151 psalms. It begins with the first psalm: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.” The Proverbs of Solomon, which begins: “The proverbs of Solomon son of David, who reigned in Israel, to know wisdom and instruction.” Ecclesiastes, by the same author, which begins: “The words of [?]

the Preacher, son of David, king of Israel in Jerusalem. Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” The Song of Songs, by the same author, which begins: “The Song of Songs, which is Solomon’s. Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine.” Job, which begins: “There was a certain man in the land of Ausitis whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and God-fearing.” The Twelve Prophets, counted as one book. They are these. Hosea comes first, and begins: “The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. The beginning of the word of the Lord in Hosea.” [?] Obadiah, which begins: “The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord God to Idumea.” Jonah, which begins: “And the word of the Lord came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying, ‘Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city.’” Nahum, which begins: “The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum of Elkosh.” Habakkuk, which begins: “The burden that Habakkuk the prophet saw.” Zephaniah, which begins: “The word of the Lord that came to Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah.” Haggai, which begins: “In the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying.” Zechariah, which begins: “In the eighth month of the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, the prophet,”

Malachi, which begins: “The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel by the hand of his messenger.” These twelve, then, make one book. After them come four others, each a book of its own. They are these. Isaiah, which begins: “The vision which Isaiah the son of Elkesaios [?] saw,

the son of Amos, which he saw concerning Judea and concerning Jerusalem in the reign of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, who reigned over Judea. Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken.” Jeremiah, which begins: “The word of God that came to Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, who was of the [?]”

Ezekiel, which begins: “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, when I was in the midst of the captivity by the river Chebar, that the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God.” Daniel, which begins: “And there was a man living in Babylon whose name was Joakim, and he took a wife named Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, who was very beautiful and feared the Lord.”

2. All together the canonical books of the Old Testament are twenty-two, the same number as the letters of the Hebrews, for that is how many letters they have. Besides these there are other books of the same Old Testament. They are not canonical and are read only to catechumens. They are these. The Wisdom of Solomon, which begins: “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth.” The Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, which begins: “All wisdom is from the Lord, and is with him for [?]”

Esther, which begins: “In the second year of the reign of Artaxerxes the Great, on the first day of Nisan, Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, had a dream.” Judith, which begins: “In the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who reigned over the Assyrians in Nineveh, the great city, in the days of Arphaxad, who reigned over the Medes in Ecbatana.” Tobit, which begins: “The book of the words of Tobit son of Tobiel, son of Ananiel, son of Aduel, son of Gabael, of the seed of Asiel, of the tribe of Naphtali, who was taken captive in the days of Enemessar king of the Assyrians.” These are all the non-canonical books. Some of the ancients, however, have said that Esther is also canonical among the Hebrews. They say that Ruth is joined with Judges and counted with it as one book, while Esther is counted as another single book. In this way the number of books that are canonical among the Hebrews again comes to twenty-two.

3. Such, and so many, are the books of the Old Testament, both canonical and non-canonical. The books of the New Testament, again defined and fixed in a canon, are these. According to Matthew, which begins: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of Abraham.” [?]

According to Luke, which begins: “Since many have undertaken to set in order an account of the matters that have been fulfilled among us.” According to John, which begins: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things came into being through him, and without him nothing that has come into being came to be.” The Acts of the Apostles, which begins: “The first account I composed, O Theophilus, about all that Jesus began both to do and to teach.” Catholic Epistles of various apostles, seven in all, counted as one book. One by James, which begins: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the dispersion, greeting.” Two by Peter. The first begins: “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the elect sojourners of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification by the Spirit, for obedience and for sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ: may grace and peace be multiplied to you.” The second begins: “Simeon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours in the righteousness of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Three by John. The first begins: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life.” The second begins: “The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth.” The third begins: “The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.” One by Jude, which begins: “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, to those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ.” The fourteen epistles of the apostle Paul, counted as one book. First, the Epistle to the Romans, which begins: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God.” Two to the Corinthians. The first begins: “Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, to the church of God that is in Corinth.” The second begins: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the church of God that is in Corinth.” Fourth, to the Galatians, which begins: “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man,

[?] through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” Fifth, to the Ephesians, which begins: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus and are faithful in Christ Jesus.” Sixth, to the Philippians, which begins: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints who are in Philippi, with the bishops and dea[cons] [?] an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae.” Two to the Thessalonians. The first begins: “Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” The second begins: “Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Tenth, the Epistle to the Hebrews, which begins: “In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son.” Two to Timothy. The first begins: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by command of God our Saviour and of Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, my true child in the faith.” The second begins: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, my beloved child.” Thirteenth, the Epistle to Titus, which begins: “Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of the truth that accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life.” Fourteenth, the Epistle to Philemon, which begins: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon our beloved fellow worker.” In addition to these there is the Revelation of John the Theologian. It was accepted as his and approved by holy, Spirit-bearing Fathers of old. It begins: “The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants what must soon take place. He made it known by sending it through his angel to his servant John.”

4. These, then, are the books of the New Testament, the canonical ones. They are, as it were, the first fruits, the anchors and the supports of our faith, since they were written and set forth by the apostles of Christ themselves, who were with him and were taught by him. Later on, following their order and in agreement with them, countless other books beyond number were produced with great labour by the great and most wise God-bearing Fathers of each age. These books bear witness to the earlier ones and shed light on them. We will not speak of them now, because they are very many and without limit, and at the same time

they all keep to the same order as these ancient books, and they too expound and clarify the same things. As has been said, then, all the books of the Old and the New Testament are included in these. So far, however, they have been listed only briefly, with regard to their number alone. From here on we must treat the same books again more fully: who wrote each of them, where it got the name it bears, and what it contains. This will be done in summary and synoptic form, following the order set out above, with each book described under its proper name.

Book 1: Genesis

5. This book of Genesis was spoken and written by Moses at the command of the Lord. It is called this because it contains the genesis of all things: of heaven and earth, of human beings and of all these visible things, and the very planting of paradise. It relates that on the first day light came into being. On the second day came the firmament, which God called heaven. On the third day the waters were gathered together and the dry land appeared. He called the gatherings of the waters seas, and the dry land he called earth, and the earth brought forth green grass and every tree. On the fourth day the sun and moon came forth, together with the whole chorus of the stars. On the fifth day came the birds, the fish and the sea monsters in the waters. On the sixth came the four-footed creatures, the wild beasts, the creeping things and the cattle, and man was formed according to the image and likeness of God. On the seventh day God rested from his works and blessed it. This book contains the transgression of Adam and his expulsion from paradise, the murder of Abel by his brother Cain, the translation of Enoch, the building of the ark, the flood that came in the time of Noah, the building of the tower, the division of tongues, the dispersion of the nations and Abraham’s departure from the Chaldeans. It also contains the overthrow of Sodom, the law concerning circumcision, the oath of God’s promise to Abraham, and the births of Isaac, of Jacob and of the patriarchs descended from him. It tells that Abraham lived 180 years and that Ishmael, born of Hagar, died at the age of 137. It tells how Joseph was sold by his brothers into Egypt, how he was slandered by his mistress and thrown into prison, and how he was later appointed ruler of all Egypt. Next it tells of the descent into Egypt of Jacob and his sons, seventy-five in number, and how Jacob, after coming there and blessing his sons the patriarchs, died at the age of 147. His body was carried away and buried in Canaan. Joseph lived for 66 years after the famine in Egypt and died at the age of 110, having first given instructions about his bones, so that they too would be carried to the tomb of his fathers.

Book 2: Exodus

6. This book of Exodus was also composed by the aforementioned Moses. It is called this because it contains the exodus of the sons of Israel from Egypt. This took place 430 years after the promise spoken to Abraham, after 215 years of sojourning in Egypt (that is how long they lived there), and after the ten plagues against Pharaoh, the tyrant of Egypt. God brought ten plagues on him, as follows. First, he turned the river into blood. Second, he brought frogs on all Egypt. Third came gnats. Fourth, the dog-fly. Fifth, the death of the livestock. Sixth, sores and boils breaking out on people and beasts. Seventh, hail and blazing fire. Eighth, locusts. Ninth, darkness over all Egypt for three days, except in the land of the sons of Israel. Tenth, the death of all the firstborn of Egypt, from people to beasts. When the people had gone out and Pharaoh pursued them, Israel crossed the Red Sea on dry ground, since the sea had been divided on either side. The Egyptians who were pursuing the people were drowned in that sea, together with Pharaoh himself. This book also contains the story of the Egyptian magicians, Jannes and Jambres, who at first opposed Moses but were later put to shame and withdrew. It contains the law concerning the Passover, the changing of the bitter water to sweet, the gift of the quail, the supply of manna from heaven, and the water brought forth for them from the rock, which Moses named Temptation and Reviling. At that time the keeping of the Sabbath also began. Here too are recorded the law given by God on Mount Sinai through Moses on two tablets of stone, and the making of the tabernacle and of the vestments of the high priest and the priests. Those who made all the works were Bezalel of the tribe of Judah and Oholiab of the tribe of Dan. The amount spent on the works was 29 [?] talents and 700 shekels of gold, 100 talents and 1,775 shekels of silver, and 70 talents and 2,500 shekels of bronze. This book also contains the transgression of the people when they made the calf below the mountain, and how Amalek was routed when Moses stretched out his hands. Then come further statutes and ordinances, and before them the ten commandments on the tablets. They are these. First: I am the Lord your God. Second: You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything. Third: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. Fourth: Remember the Sabbath day. Fifth: Honour your father and your mother. Sixth: You shall not murder. Seventh: You shall not commit adultery. Eighth: You shall not steal. Ninth: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour. Tenth: You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife, nor anything that belongs to your neighbour. When the tabernacle was com-

pleted, it was set up in the second year of their exodus, at the new moon of the first month. With these things the book of Exodus concludes.

Book 3: Leviticus

7. This book of Leviticus was also composed by the aforementioned Moses. It is named this because it contains, in particular, the whole ordering of the Levitical service. It tells how Aaron and his sons are chosen from the tribe of Levi and anointed as priests. It sets out all the different kinds of sacrifices and offerings, the character of all the worship in the sanctuary, and the Levitical and priestly service, as well as the law of each sacrifice. It deals with the peace offering and with voluntary and involuntary trespasses, and explains how each offering must be divided and offered up. This book also deals with the anointing of the high priest and the priests. It covers how to discern and recognize the signs of leprosy in people, in garments and in the walls of a house, and the law for their cleansing. It gives the law on marriages, distinguishing which are lawful and which are unlawful. It also distinguishes clean from unclean cattle, birds and fish, that is, which of them the Hebrews were to eat and which they were to abstain from. It appoints the day of trumpets for the new moon of the seventh month. It gives the command of the great fast, which they are to keep in the same seventh month, on the tenth of the month, and which it calls a sabbath of sabbaths and a remission of sin. It also contains the feast of Tabernacles on the fifteenth of the same month. It gives instructions about the feasts and the offerings that must be brought at them, about the release of Hebrews who have been sold, about the cancelling of debts, and about the rest of the land, which is to take place every seven years. It also contains a reminder of the statutes, ordinances and testimonies, with promises to those who keep them and the most terrible threats against those who transgress them. It distinguishes clean from unclean foods, and gives the reason, as follows. Among cattle it calls clean those that part the hoof, are cloven-footed with two claws, and chew the cud: for example, the calf, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the oryx, the buffalo, the white-rumped antelope, the goat-stag, the giraffe and the like. If any of these marks was missing in an animal, it was unclean: for example, the camel, the hare and the rock badger, for these chew the cud but do not part the hoof. The pig is also unclean, for it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed but does not chew the cud. As for birds, those it forbids to be eaten are these: the eagle, the griffon, the sea eagle, the vulture, the kite and those like them; the raven and those like it; the ostrich, the owl, the gull and those like them; the hawk and those like it; the night raven, the cormorant, the ibis, the purple gallinule, the pelican, the swan, the heron, the plover and those like them; the hoopoe, and [?]

bat. Of winged creeping things, he says that all those are unclean which go on four feet but have legs above their feet so that they can leap with them from the ground, such as the brouchos-locust, the attacus, the locust and the like, and the ophiomachus. Of creatures born in the waters, whether in the sea, in rivers or in torrents, he says that those are clean which have fins and scales, such as the red mullet, the parrotfish, the glaucus, the grey mullet and the like. Those that lack either of these are unclean, or rather not to be eaten, such as cuttlefish: they have fins but no scales. Of the creeping things on the land he says these are unclean: the weasel, the land crocodile, the shrew, the chameleon, the gecko, the lizard and the mole. It was unnecessary to mention the serpent and the like, for, he says, it is plain that these are abominable and hateful to everyone; yet he did mention them in Deuteronomy.

Book 4: Numbers. 8. This book too, the composition called Numbers, is by the same Moses. The book is so called because it contains the number of the whole people, each tribe of the Jews being counted by command of the Lord. The people were numbered from twenty years old and upward, every man able to go out to war, apart from the tribe of Levi, which was counted by itself. The number of those counted came to six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty. Those who numbered the people were Moses and Aaron, and with them the leader of each tribe. The names of the leaders and the numbers are these. Of Reuben, Elizur son of Shedeur; their number was forty-six thousand five hundred. Of Simeon, Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai; their number was seventy-four thousand six hundred. Of Issachar, Nethanel son of Zuar; their number was fifty-four thousand four hundred. Of Zebulun, Eliab son of Helon; their number was fifty-seven thousand four hundred. Of the sons of Joseph, of Ephraim, Elishama son of Ammihud; their number was forty thousand five hundred. Of Manasseh, Gamaliel son of Pedahzur; their number was thirty-two thousand three hundred. Of Benjamin, [?] son of Gideon; their number was thirty-five thousand four hundred. [Note: Num. 2:22, “Abidan son of Gideoni.”]

Of Dan, Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai; their number was sixty-four thousand seven hundred. Of Asher, Pagiel son of Ochran; their number was forty-one thousand five hundred. Of Gad, Eliasaph son of Reuel; their number was forty-five thousand six hundred and fifty. Of Naphtali, Ahira son of Enan; their number was fifty-three thousand four hundred. This is the number of the fighting men: six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty. The tribe of Levi was numbered separately, at the word of the Lord, by Moses and Aaron alone, from a month old and upward; their number was twenty-two thousand. Moses alone also numbered the male firstborn of all the other tribes, and their number came to twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three. In place of these firstborn the Levites were reckoned as belonging to God, for the Levites were about as many. They too are ordered to be purified by Moses, and are then set apart through Aaron to do the work of the Lord on behalf of the people, to carry the furnishings of the tabernacle, and to minister to Aaron and his sons. This book also contains the arrangement of the people's march, the setting up of the tabernacle, and the command about the trumpets, by which the people were to be summoned. Here too is recorded the dedication of the altar, how he anointed the tabernacle and consecrated it and everything in it; the order of the offerings for the dedication of the altar; and the limit set on the years of the Levites' service: they were to begin serving at twenty-five years of age, and at fifty were to retire from the service and only guard the tabernacle. There is written also the account of the water of conviction that brings the curse, and the law about those who vow to abstain from wine and not to cut their hair; and how, when the people once grumbled for meat, God gave them quail, and when they were thirsty and grumbled again, he gave them water from the rock, which Moses called the water of contradiction. He sent out spies, one from each tribe, among them Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh. Here too the company of Korah rose up against Moses and were swallowed alive into the earth together with Dathan and Abiram; it was then also that Miriam, Aaron's sister, became leprous, and Aaron's rod budded with almonds. After this Aaron dies on Mount Hor, and his son Eleazar succeeds him. Here also is told the story of Balaam and his [?] that spoke with a human voice; and how Balak, king of Moab, was put to shame; and how, when the people had been defiled at Balaam's suggestion, Phinehas ran through the Midianite woman and

the Israelite Zimri of the tribe of Simeon for their fornication, and so the wrath was stopped. When the people spoke against Moses to God, they were bitten by snakes; afterwards, when they pleaded, God ordered a bronze serpent to be made and hung up, so that anyone who was bitten might look at it and live. Here God commands Moses and Eleazar the priest to number the people again from twenty years old and upward, and their number came to six hundred and one thousand seven hundred and thirty. The Levites were again numbered by themselves and came to twenty-three thousand. This census took place in the plains of Moab, by the Jordan opposite Jericho. Among those counted there was none of those counted earlier, for they had died, except Caleb and Joshua son of Nun. In this book Moses wrote down, at the word of the Lord, their departures and the stations where they stopped to rest on their journey from Egypt. They are these. They set out from Rameses in Egypt in the first month, on the day after the Passover, and came to Succoth; from Succoth to Buthan; from Buthan to Baal-zephon, opposite Migdol; from Baal-zephon they crossed through the middle of the sea; from the sea to the Bitter Waters; from the Bitter Waters to Elim, where the palm trees are; from Elim to Seir, the wilderness; from the wilderness of Seir to Rhairaca; from Rhairaca to Elim; from Elim to Rephidim; from Rephidim to the wilderness of Sinai; from the wilderness of Sinai to the Graves of Craving; from the Graves of Craving to Hazeroth; from Hazeroth to Rithmah; from Rithmah to Rimmon-perez; from Rimmon-perez to Lemona; from Lemona to Dessa; from Dessa to Makellath; from Makellath to Saphar; from Saphar to Charadath; from Charadath to Makheloth; from Makheloth to Kateka; from Matteka to Selmona; from Selmona to Masuroth; from Masuroth to Banaia; from Banaia to Mount Gadgad; from Mount Gadgad to Etabatha; from Etabatha to Sebrona; from Sebrona to Ezion-geber; from Ezion-geber to the wilderness of Zin; and from the wilderness of Zin to the wilderness of Paran, which is Kadesh. There Miriam died, at Kadesh. From Kadesh to Hor, the mountain near the land of Edom, up which Aaron the high priest went and died at the Lord's command, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel came out of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month, at the age of a hundred and twenty-three. From Mount Hor to Selmona; from Selmona to Phino; from Phino to Oboth; from Oboth to Gai, in the region beyond, on the borders of Moab; from Gai to Dibon-gad; from Dibon-gad to Gelmon-diblathaim; and from Gelmon-diblathaim to the mountains [?]

of Abarim, opposite Nebo; from the mountains of Abarim to the west of Moab, by the Jordan opposite Jericho; and they encamped beside the Jordan. The stations number forty-three. Here Moses, having routed and subdued the nations beyond the Jordan, after Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, who was one of the giants, had been killed, is commanded to distribute the lands to Reuben, to Gad and to half the tribe of Manasseh, and to instruct the children of Israel to give the Levites, out of the portions of their own possession, cities to live in along with the pasture lands around the cities; and further to provide cities of refuge, three beyond the Jordan and three in the land of Canaan, so that anyone who had killed unintentionally might flee there and not be killed rashly by a kinsman of the slain, until he stood before the congregation for judgment. In this book the people are commanded to make tassels on their garments, and on the tassels a thread of blue, so that when they see them they may not forget the commandments of God. Here the daughters of Zelophehad receive an inheritance, that of their father; and from their case there arises a command of the Lord and a law that marriage between cousins is lawful. Here also Moses saw the promised land from Mount Abarim, that is, Nebo, and heard: “You shall not enter there, because of the provocation at the water of contradiction.” Aaron died at the age of a hundred and twenty-three, in the fortieth year after the exodus, in the fifth month. As for those sent to spy out the land, one man was sent from each tribe by command of the Lord, and their names are these: of the tribe of Reuben, Salamiel son of Zaccur; of the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat son of Surei; of the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh; of the tribe of Issachar, Ilaal son of Joseph; of the tribe of Ephraim, Nauses son of Nun; of the tribe of Benjamin, Palti son of Raphu; of the tribe of Zebulun, Gudiel son of Sodi; of the tribe of Joseph, of the sons of Manasseh, Gaddi son of Susi; of the tribe of Dan, Amies son of Gamai; of the tribe of Asher, Sethur son of Michael; of the tribe of Naphtali, [?] son of Nabi; of the tribe of Gad, Gaddidudiel [?] son of Machi. The place from which they were sent is Paran and Kadesh-barnea. It was then that Moses gave Nauses son of Nun the name Joshua. The season in which they were sent was the middle of spring, when the first grapes appear; the time they spent spying out the land was forty days

to the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant he had made with them at Horeb. This is why the tablets are said to belong to Horeb and were placed inside the ark, whereas this book Moses ordered the priests who carried the ark to place at the side of the ark as a testimony; and he ordered it to be read every seven years, on the day of release, when the Feast of Tabernacles was also held. This is the first reason for the book's name. There is also a second, different reason: in it he repeats and explains everything said earlier in Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers — the ordinances, judgments and commandments — and reminds the people again to keep them. In it he also recounts once more the exodus from Egypt and all the benefits done for them, and the signs and wonders, so that they might not forget the God who had done them. In it he also gives directions about the blessing for those who keep the law and the curse for those who break it: the blessing was to be pronounced on Mount Gerizim by Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin, and the curse on Mount Ebal by Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali. As a reminder and for constant meditation he wrote, by the Lord's command, the great Song, so that by learning it by heart and meditating on it continually they might not forget God. Having blessed each tribe and written down the blessing, and having laid his hands on Joshua son of Nun so that he might succeed him according to God's command, he finally went up Mount Abarim, that is, Nebo, and died there at the word of the Lord at the age of a hundred and twenty, his eyes undimmed and his face unimpaired; and no one knows his burial place to this day.

Book 6: Joshua son of Nun. 10. The books from here up to Ezra are not all the compositions of those whose names they bear in their titles and about whom they speak; the tradition is that they were written by the prophets of the respective periods. For now, then, we must discuss their titles. The present book is entitled Joshua son of Nun because Joshua son of Nun himself succeeded Moses and led the people, and the book contains his history and his deeds. In this book is told how the waters of the river Jordan coming down from its source stood still, while the water that had already passed drained away, and they crossed it dry-shod; how at Gilgal he circumcised with stone knives all who had been born in the wilderness, and called the place Gilgal; how, once the people had crossed and eaten of the produce of the land, the manna ceased; how the walls of Jericho fell of their own accord, while Rahab the harlot was saved because she had protected the spies; and how the sun, standing at mid-heaven, at the prayer of Joshua son of Nun stood still over Gibeon for the space of a whole day, until he had routed the ene-

mies. Having defeated the Amorites and Manedoth [?], king of Jokneam of Carmel, king [?] king of Tirzah.

Book 7: Judges. 11. The book is called Judges because after the death of Joshua son of Nun, God saved the people through the judges when they were oppressed by foreigners, that is, by the Canaanites who had been left; and this book contains both the deeds of each of these judges and the length of his life. The judges were these. First, Othniel: he killed Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, who had oppressed the people for forty years. After him Ehud, who was ambidextrous: he killed Eglon, king of Moab, with a two-edged sword a span long, [?] the people [?]. [Notes: [?]; another reading: Aphek of Arok; another reading: eight years; another reading: Aod.]

eighteen years; and he judged Israel eighty years. After him Shamgar son of Anath: he struck down six hundred of the foreigners with an ox-goad, and he judged the people for one year. After him Barak son of Abinoam: he fought Jabin and Sisera, who had oppressed Israel for twenty years. Sisera was killed with a tent peg by Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite; and Barak judged Israel forty years. After him Gideon, who is Jerubbaal: he struck down Midian and its rulers Oreb, Zebah and Zalmunna, overthrew the tower of Penuel, and threshed their rulers with thorns — they who had oppressed Israel for seven years. He judged Israel forty years. After him Abimelech, Gideon's son by a concubine: he killed his brothers, the sons of the free wives, seventy men on a single stone. One of them, Jotham, escaped. But Abimelech, together with those who had joined him, became like fire from a bramble; and after killing many, he too died when a woman threw a piece of millstone on him from the wall. He ruled three years. After him Tola son of Puah, the son of Abimelech's uncle; he ruled twenty-three years. After him Jair the Gileadite, twenty-two years. After him Jephthah the Gileadite: he killed the Ammonites and the Philistines, who had oppressed Israel for eighteen years. He had vowed during the war to offer as a sacrifice whoever first came out to meet him after the victory; his daughter met him, and she asked first to be granted two months to mourn her virginity. Her father then offered her as a sacrifice, and he judged the people six years. After him Ibzan of Bethlehem, seven years. After him Elon the Zebulunite, ten years. After him Abdon the Pirathonite, eight years. After him Samson of Dan: he struck down the Philistines with the jawbone of an ass, another time with a rod, again with foxes, and finally with the collapse of the house — they who had oppressed Israel for forty years. He judged Israel twenty years. The judges number thirteen in all, and their years four hundred and eleven.

Book 8: Ruth. 12. The book is so called because it contains only the story of Ruth. Ruth was a Moabitess by birth and distinguished for her virtue. Renouncing her kindred and her ancestral superstition, she turned to the worship of God and went straight to Bethlehem in Judea. There she was married to Boaz, who was of the tribe of Judah, and from her David's descent is traced as follows: Boaz by Ruth begets Obed, Obed begets Jesse, and Jesse begets David.

Book 9: Kingdoms, First and Second. 13. The books are called Kingdoms because they contain the deeds of the kings who reigned in Judah and in Israel, and their years. In the first book of Kingdoms the following are [Note: another reading: Abineem.]

treated: the death of Eli the priest and his sons; the birth of Samuel; and how the people, who had formerly been ruled by God, who raised up a deliverer for them as each occasion required, nevertheless asked Samuel for a king after the custom of the nations, and he gave them Saul of the tribe of Benjamin; and from then on kingship began in Israel too. It also tells how Saul broke God's command and the kingdom was taken from his line, while David was anointed in his place and the kingdom passed to his line. David killed Goliath with a very small stone; and because the dancing women gave the tens of thousands to David and the thousands to Saul, Saul grew jealous and pursued David. David escaped, but Saul, hard pressed in war, sought out mediums, and the next day he was killed and died. With this the first book of Kingdoms ends.

14. In the second, David in turn succeeded to the kingdom. At first Saul's son Mephibosheth contested it, wanting to reign, but later everyone went over to David. David was victorious in all his wars. He took Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah; his son Absalom pursued him, and not long afterwards, when battle was joined, Absalom was killed. Then, by numbering the people, he provoked God's wrath against himself; but afterwards, when God had been entreated, the wrath ceased. The second book of Kingdoms closes at this point, with David grown old. David had mighty men under him, great and many, so that the least of them was a match for a hundred and the greatest for a thousand. The names and deeds of some of them are these. Sebochai the Astothite: he struck down Ser, son of Rapha, a descendant of the giants. Elhanan son of Ariorgi, the Bethlehemite: he struck down Goliath the Hittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam; he too was a son of Rapha. Jonathan son of Shimei, David's brother: he struck down a man from Rameda who taunted Israel, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot; he too was a son of Rapha, a descendant of the giants. Adinon the Asonite: he drew his sword against eight hundred soldiers at once. Iessaibada son of Achamane: he too drew his sword against three hundred slain at one time. Elhanan son of Sose: when the foreigners had gathered, he leapt on them alone and kept killing them until his spear stuck fast to his hand, while the people behind him took the spoils. Mara son of Asa, the Sarouchite: when the foreigners came and wanted to seize a plot of field full of lentils, and the people had fled, he alone stood his ground, drove off the foreigners, and guarded the plot of field.

Eleazar, son of Dodo the Archonite [?]. When there was a plot of barley, and the Philistines attacked and the people fled, he alone stood his ground. He routed the Philistines and saved the barley. Three mighty men from among the thirty were with David. The Philistines had surrounded Bethlehem, and David longed to drink from the cistern in Bethlehem. So the three went over, broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the cistern and brought it to David. David marveled at their might and accepted the water, but he would not drink it. Instead he poured it out to the Lord, saying: “Far be it from me, Lord, to do this! Shall I drink the blood of men who went at the risk of their lives?” Benaiah son of Jehoiada did many mighty deeds. He struck down the sons of Ariel of Moab, and he went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed the lion. He also struck down a mighty Egyptian who was five cubits tall and had a spear like a weaver's beam. He snatched the spear from him and killed him with it. Abishai, brother of Joab, was the son of Zeruiah, David's sister. He too was a chief among the three just mentioned. On one occasion he struck down thirty men with the spear, and he ran like a gazelle on the mountains. He also struck down and killed Ishbi, who wanted to kill David. Ishbi was a descendant of Rapha. He had a spear weighing thirty shekels of bronze, and he was girded with a club. These, then, were the great and mighty men. In all, David had three hundred and forty thousand two hundred warriors. Book 10: Kingdoms, Third and Fourth. 15. The third book, then, tells further how, when David had grown old, his son Adonijah exalted himself and proclaimed himself king without his father. When David learned of this, he sent Nathan the prophet, Zadok the priest and Benaiah son of Jehoiada and gave them his orders, and they anointed Solomon king while David was still alive. Adonijah was put down at once. Solomon succeeded to the throne and built the house of the Lord and the wall of Jerusalem in seven years. He had seventy thousand burden-bearers from among the proselytes, and eighty thousand stonecutters, also from the proselytes. Over the works he had three thousand [?] twenty overseers. Twelve men provided their food and necessities, each for one month. Their daily provision was thirty cors of fine flour, sixty cors of ground meal, ten choice calves, twenty pasture-fed oxen and a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles and choice fattened fowl. He had a herd of forty thousand brood mares, and twelve thousand horses for chariots. He had great wealth: in a single year the gold brought to him weighed 666 [?] talents, apart from the tribute of his subjects. The queen of Sheba also came to him and gave him a hundred and twenty talents of gold, and [?] nine, six hundred [?]

precious stones and countless spices. After Solomon's death his son Rehoboam succeeded to the kingdom, and under him the realm was split. Ten tribes went off to Samaria, and two remained in Jerusalem, Judah and Benjamin. This third book, then, contains the acts and years of the following kings. First, Solomon, king over all together. Then, after the division of the kingdom described above, the kings of the two tribes in Judea: Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa and Jehoshaphat. And the kings of the ten tribes in Samaria: Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri and Ahab. It also deals with these prophets: Nathan and Gad, Ahijah the Shilonite, and the one who cried out against the altar of Samaria. It deals with Elijah and Elisha, with the one who prophesied to Ahab about the son of Hadad, and with the one who struck him and rebuked Ahab. It also tells that there were sons of the prophets who lived apart by themselves. This book also tells how Elijah prophesied and it did not rain for three years, and how by the word of the Lord ravens brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening. In Zarephath of Sidon, by the word of the Lord, he kept the widow's jar of flour from running out and her flask of oil from running low. By his prayer he raised her son, who had died, and he had the prophets of Baal put to death, 459 of them. He struck the Jordan with his mantle, and the water was divided this way and that, and he crossed the river on foot. This book ends with the death of Ahab king of Israel, the death of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, the beginning of the reign of Ahaziah son of Ahab, and the beginning of the reign of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah. Book 4 of Kingdoms. 18. The fourth book tells how Ahaziah's two captains of fifty were consumed by fire at the word of Elijah the prophet. It tells how Elijah was taken up, how the spirit of Elijah rested on Elisha, and how he received a double share of the spirit. It tells how Elisha raised the dead son of the Shunammite woman by his prayer, cleansed Naaman the Syrian of leprosy, and filled the vessels of the prophet's wife with oil by the word of the Lord. After his death a dead man, girded only in a loincloth, was thrown onto his bones, and as soon as he touched the prophet's bones he came back to life. Elisha also struck the Jordan with Elijah's mantle, and the water was divided this way and that, and he too crossed on foot. This book also tells how Sennacherib and Rabshakeh, after much blasphemy, were driven off, and a hundred and eighty-five thousand of their men were destroyed in one night. King Josiah tore down all the idols, cut down the sacred groves and kept the Passover lawfully, as it is written. The book also contains the acts and years of the kings. In Judea these were Jehoram, Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah and

Jehoahaz, Eliakim, Jehoiachin, and Mattaniah, also called Zedekiah. In Samaria they were Ahaziah, Jehoram, Jehu, Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam, Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah and Hoshea. The book also deals with the prophets Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah and Jeremiah. It tells that the kingdom of Samaria came to an end under Hoshea son of Elah, who had slain Pekah son of Remaliah, and that the kingdom of Jerusalem came to an end under Zedekiah. Zedekiah was led away to Babylon, and his eyes were put out, and he was thrown into the mill for twenty-six [?] years. After this the king of Babylon raised up Jehoiachin. He gave him a throne above the other kings who were there, and Jehoiachin ate and drank with him all the days of his life. The book ends here, with the people taken captive and the whole city captured. Summary of the Acts of the Kings of Judea and Israel. 17. We must now take up the account again from the beginning. We will set out in summary the names, acts and years of reign of all the kings, both of the Jews and of Samaria, beginning with the kings of Jerusalem. After the death of Saul, who reigned forty years, David reigned over all Israel, also for forty years: seven years in Hebron, and thirty-three over all Israel and Judah. He did what was right with a perfect heart. In his time the prophets were Samuel, Nathan and Gad. Solomon son of David reigned over all the people, also for forty years. He did evil. In his time the prophets were Nathan and Gad. Rehoboam his son reigned seventeen years. He did evil. Under him the kingdom was split: two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, remained with him in Jerusalem, and ten tribes were in Samaria. In his time the prophets were Ahijah the Shilonite, Shemaiah and Iddo. Abijah his son, three years. His heart was not perfect like David's, but he walked in the sins of his father. In his time Iddo was the prophet. Asa his son, forty-one years. He did what was right, but the high places still remained. In his time the prophets were Azariah son of Oded, and Hanani. Jehoshaphat his son, twenty-five years. He did what was right, but the high places still remained. Later he was blamed for lawlessness, because he made friends with Ahaziah king of Israel and went into partnership with him in a shipping venture. In his time the prophets were Elijah, Elisha, Micaiah, Jehu son of Hanani, Jahaziel son of Zechariah, and Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah. Jehoram his son, eight years. He did evil, for his wife was a daughter of Ahab. In his time were Elijah and Elisha. Ahaziah his son, one year. He did evil. After him came Athaliah his mother, seven years. Joash son of Ahaziah, forty years. He murdered Zechariah. He did what was right as long as the wise Jehoiada lived and enlightened him. His servants killed him in

the house of Millo. In his time Azariah [Zechariah] son of Jehoiada prophesied. Amaziah his son, twenty-nine [?] years. At first he did what was right, but not like David, for the people still sacrificed on the high places, and he did not remove the sacred groves. Prophets prophesied in his time, but their names were not recorded. Later, however, Amaziah struck down the people of Seir and grew proud. He served the idols of Seir, and he was struck down and handed over to his enemies. Azariah, who is Uzziah, fifty-two years. At first he did what was right, as his father had, except that he did not remove the high places. But as he prospered he grew proud and wanted to burn incense himself in the temple, which is permitted only to the priests. So he became leprous, after hearing the words: “It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated.” In his time Isaiah prophesied. Jotham his son, sixteen years. He did what was right, as his father had, except that he did not remove the high places. In his time was Isaiah. Ahaz his son, sixteen years. He did evil. In his time Isaiah and Oded were prophets. Hezekiah his son, twenty-nine years. He did what was right, perfectly, as David had. He destroyed the bronze serpent that Moses had hung up. In his time was Isaiah. In his time the Assyrians Sennacherib and Rabshakeh blasphemed. They themselves were later struck down, and in one night an angel went out and destroyed a hundred and eighty-five thousand of their men. Hezekiah fell ill and was about to die, but he was given fifteen more years. Manasseh his son, fifty-five years. He did evil: whatever Hezekiah had torn down, Manasseh rebuilt. He became another Jeroboam to Judah, so that because of him Jerusalem suffered as Samaria had. For it was said of him: “He made Judah sin.” So he was led away captive to Babylon. But in his captivity, as it is written in Chronicles, he repented, and God brought him back to Jerusalem, and he took up the kingdom again. He died repenting and teaching the people to serve God. He was not buried in the city of David but in his garden, the garden of Uzza. Amon his son reigned two years. He did evil, as his father Manasseh had. His servants killed him, and he was buried in the garden of Uzza, where his father also lay. Josiah his son, thirty-one years. The people made him king when he was eight years old. He did what was right in all the way of David and turned aside neither to the right nor to the left. At the age of sixteen he cut down the sacred groves and tore down all the idols. He searched for the law and, finding that it had been neglected, had it read aloud. He proclaimed the Passover and kept it as it is written. Pharaoh Neco killed him at the Euphrates after Josiah had contended with him. In his time the prophets were Jeremiah and Zephaniah, and Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum. Jehoahaz his son, three months. He did evil, and Pharaoh Neco removed him. In his time was Jere-

-miah. Eliakim, another son of Josiah, who was renamed Jehoiakim, eleven years. He did evil. Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, his son, three months. He did evil and was led away to Babylon. Mattaniah his son. Nebuchadnezzar made him king and renamed him Zedekiah. He reigned eleven years and did evil. In his time was Jeremiah. Up to this king the kingdom of Judah held power, and then it was destroyed, as Samaria's had been. The city was captured, and all were led away captive to Babylon with [?]. Altogether there were twenty-one kings of Jerusalem from David to the Babylonian captivity. This of course does not count Athaliah, who also reigned for seven years after the death of her son Ahaziah, as has been said. The Kings of Israel. 18. Next we must speak of the kings of Israel in Samaria: what each of them was called, how many years he reigned, and how

The first to reign in Samaria, when the kingdom was split, was Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had come up from Egypt. He did evil as no one else did. Fearing that he would be overthrown, he made two golden heifers and deceived the people, saying: “These are the gods who brought us up out of Egypt.” He also invented priests for them, and so he made Israel sin, for all who came after him followed his example. He reigned twenty-four years. In his time the prophets were Ahijah the Shilonite and the man who cried out against him at the altar. Nadab [?] his son, two years. He did evil, and no one of his family reigned after him. Baasha, of another family, twenty-four years. He did evil. Elah [?] his son, two years. He did evil, and no one of his family reigned after him. Zimri, of another family, twelve years. He did evil. Ahab his son, twenty-two years. He did more evil than the others. In his time the prophets were Elijah, Elisha and Micaiah. There were also the one who prophesied to Ahab about Syria and the son of Hadad, and the one who struck him with a wound and rebuked Ahab, and many sons of the prophets living apart by themselves. Ahaziah his son, two years. He did evil. In his time were Elijah and Elisha, for it was his captains of fifty whom Elijah struck with fire at the word of the Lord. Jehoram, another son of Ahab, twelve years. He did evil, and no one of his family reigned after him. Elijah was taken up in his time; [?]

but Elisha lived on until Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. In their time there were also sons of the prophets. Jehu son of Nimshi, of another family, twenty-eight years. He wiped out the family of Ahab and destroyed the prophets of Baal by a trick, and he smashed Baal's pillar. Because he did what was right in this, he received a promise: “Your sons to the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel.” Yet he did not keep the law with his whole heart, for he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam over the heifers. Jehoahaz his son, seventeen years. He did evil. Joash his son, sixteen years. He did evil. He made war on Jerusalem and took the gold and the vessels. Jeroboam his son, forty-one years. He did evil. Zechariah his son, six months. He did evil. Up to him, the family of Jehu had sons to the fourth generation. Shallum son of Jabesh, of another family, thirty days. He did evil. Menahem son of Gadi, of another family, twenty years. He did evil. Pekahiah his son, ten years. He did evil. In his time Isaiah and Hosea were prophesying. Pekah son of Remaliah, of another family, twenty years. He slew Pekahiah and did evil. In his time the prophets were Isaiah and Hosea. Hoshea son of Elah, of another family, nine years. He slew Pekah and did evil, though not like those before him. With this Hoshea the kingdom of Samaria came to its end. From then on it ceased to exist and Samaria perished. Afterwards Assyrians settled there, and from them came the heretical Samaritans, who are also called Sadducees [read: Cuthaeans]. So the years of those who reigned in Jerusalem, from David to Zedekiah inclusive, add up to four hundred in all. The kings number twenty-one in all, not counting Athaliah. All were of a single family, David's, son succeeding father, inheriting the kingdom from beginning to end. Of these, nine did what was right and twelve did evil, not counting

Of those who reigned in Samaria, from Jeroboam to Hoshea, the years add up to two hundred and sixty-eight in all. The kings number eighteen in all, but they came from different families. Eight of them rose to rule, and all of them did evil, following the sin

Book 11: Chronicles (Paralipomena, “Things Left Out”), First and Second. 19. These books are given this name because they contain many things that were left out of Kingdoms. The first book contains a genealogy of all the tribes from Adam down to the kings, arranged by tribes, by clans, by families and by households. The second deals with the acts of the kings.

It was said earlier that the acts and the chronology of the kings were written down by the prophets of each period. So that each of them may be known, we have noted the following from Chronicles. The acts of David were written by the prophets Samuel, Nathan and Gad. Those of Solomon were written by the prophets Nathan and Ahijah. Those of Jeroboam were written by the prophets Shemaiah and Iddo. Those of Abijah were written by Iddo the prophet. Those of Asa are in the Book of the Words of the Kings of Judah. Those of Jehoshaphat were written by Jehu the prophet, son of Hanani, who wrote down the Book of the Words of the Kings of Judah. Those of Joash are in the writing of the Kingdoms. Those of Amaziah are in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. Those of Uzziah were written by Isaiah the prophet. Those of Jotham are in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. Those of Ahaz are in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. Those of Hezekiah were written by Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz. Those of Manasseh are in the Words of the Seers. Those of Josiah are in the Book of the Kings of Judah. Those of Jehoiakim are in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. Book 12 [?]: Esdras, First and Second. 20. These two books were written by the very man whose name they bear in their title. This Ezra, a priest and reader, recounts the return of the children of Israel from Persia to Jerusalem. In the book he tells how the return came about under the leadership of Jeshua son of Jozadak, Ezra, Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, a Jewish eunuch. The occasion of the return was this. Three soldiers who guarded the king, one of whom was Zerubbabel, held a contest over a question. The promise was made that the winner could ask the king for whatever he wished. One said that wine was strongest, and the second said that the king was strongest. Zerubbabel maintained that women were strongest, and truth above all. Because this answer won, he was told to ask for whatever he wanted. He asked that the captives be released and that Jerusalem be rebuilt. It happened as he asked, and the captives were released. For at that time the sixty years of wrath were also fulfilled. Those who came up from the captivity, from Judah and Benjamin, together with all the Levites, numbered forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty in all. Their male and female servants numbered 7,334 [?], the singers 245, the camels 435 and the donkeys 6,728. The builders were Zerubbabel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, and Nehemiah. Ezra, who was learned in the law, brought out the law himself and read it. He set in order everything concerning the temple and instructed the Levites from the law. He also had the foreign wives sent away by the men who had married them during the captivity. They all sent them away and were purified, and they kept the Passover lawfully, as it is written, and the fast [?].

In the second book he again says the same things about the return, but without the problems. He explains more about Nehemiah the eunuch: that he too made petition about the building of the temple, and that Ezra read aloud, while Jeshua, Banaiah and Abiah were instructing the people. Ezra, as he read, set out the knowledge of the Lord distinctly; the people understood the reading, and they kept the Passover. In the seventh month they kept the fast and the Feast of Tabernacles, as it is written: "For," it says, "they had not done so since the days of Joshua son of Nun." When Ezra saw that women of Azotus had intermarried with the Hebrews, he mourned and wept, and he made everyone promise to keep the law of God. He cast out the women as unlawful [?], and all swore to keep the law. Sanctified and purified in this way, they rejoiced, [?] and each went away to his own house. This too is recorded about Ezra: when the books had been lost through the people's negligence and because of the long captivity, Ezra himself, being a lover of learning, gifted, and a reader, preserved them all by himself. He then brought them out and published them to everyone, and so the books are preserved. Book 13: the Psalter of David. [?] The book of Psalms bears David's title [?], but it also contains psalms by many others: namely by Asaph, by Jeduthun, by the sons of Korah, by Haggai and Zechariah, and by Heman the Israelite. There are also some that were spoken by all of them together, namely those that have "Alleluia." Ezra gathered all these psalms spoken by each of them and put them together into one book. Because everything it contains is held in common, it is called the Book of Psalms. It is titled with David's name alone, however, because he was the first to receive from God the spirit of psalmody, and the first to compose and write psalms. He also chose the other psalmists mentioned above from among the priests and organized them. He fixed and arranged their positions, the order of the singing, and the times, morning and evening. Some stood when the temple was opened and others when it was closed, some on the right and others on the left. In this way some sang psalms and praised, sang and hymned God, while others struck up thanksgiving and praise. Some sounded forth on lyres, harps and cymbals, and others raised the sound with trumpets. The priests who brought up the ark in David's time were one thousand and two, as follows: of the sons of Kohath, Uriel the chief and his brothers, 110; of the sons of Merari, Ase the chief and his brothers, 250; of the sons of Gedeon, Joel the chief and his brothers, 150; of the sons of Elisaphat, Shemaiah the chief and his brothers, 200; of the sons of Hebron, Ener the chief and his brothers, 80; of the sons of Eziel, Amminadab the chief and his brothers, 112. The psalmists chosen from among them were those already mentioned, and they were arranged as follows: Asaph and Aitham, sons of Korah, with

bronze cymbals, sounding aloud so as to be heard by all. Zechariah and Oziel, Samiramoth, Eloni, Eliab, Maaseiah and Banaiah, those of Jeduthun, with harps and psaltery.
