So this book contains the knowledge of wisdom and instruction, the understanding of words of prudence, turns of speech, the understanding of true righteousness, the directing of judgments, and the promise that from these one will know parables, sayings of the wise, riddles and dark words. It contains the knowledge of wisdom and instruction because the Greeks profess to have wisdom, and the heretics think they have instruction. That is why he teaches the true wisdom and instruction, so that no one, because of the shared name of wisdom, may fall into the sophistries of the Greeks and the heretics. For some of the Greeks, thinking themselves to be something, "claimed to be wise and became fools." The heretics, thinking they are instructed, have been perverted, and they sin, being self-condemned. But the wise man who hears the divine words will become wiser. Whoever has heard the ordinances of God and kept them, and has not made light of the Lord's discipline nor lost heart under it, will become a wise son. Once he is instructed, he will quickly receive the knowledge of God as well, for this is what the wise are taught. The understanding of words of prudence is the teaching about the only and true God. Among the Greeks, some said God was a body, while others likened him to idols. The heretics, too, have gone mad concerning Him who is. That is why he expounds the true knowledge of God. Of God's ineffability he says: "The glory of God conceals a word." Of his providence he says: "In every place the eyes of the Lord watch the evil and the good"; and again: "The rich and the poor have met one another, and the Lord made them both"; and: "When lender and debtor meet together, the Lord watches over them both"; and: "For a man's ways are before the eyes of God, and he watches all his paths." Of his role as judge he says: "The sacrifices of the ungodly are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of the upright are acceptable to him"; and again: "The Lord pulls down the houses of the insolent, but he has set up the widow's boundary." He speaks of God's creative work not in general terms, but says that God makes all things through his own Word and Wisdom. This above all marks out the true God: that he is the Father of a Son. So he says: "God founded the earth by wisdom"; and again: "The Lord made lands and uninhabited places, and the inhabited heights of the world under heaven. When he prepared the heaven, I was present with him; when he marked out his throne upon the winds, when he made strong the clouds above, I was beside him, setting all in order. I was the one [?] in whom he delighted, and day by day I rejoiced in his presence." They are called "turns of speech" because when one turns them over in the mind, one opens them up and finds the sense that lies within them. Examples are: "An understanding son is kept safe from the heat, but a lawless son is blasted by the wind at harvest"; and again: "Take care of the green things in the field, and you will cut grass; gather the mountain hay, so that you may have sheep for clothing";

and again: "If you sit down to dine at the table of rulers, consider wisely what is set before you"; and the like. "The understanding of true righteousness" is said because people have understood justice in different ways. Some say that justice is returning what one has received for safekeeping. Others say it is giving evil for evil and good for good. But such definitions turn out not to be exact, for "Do not say: As he treated me, so I will treat him, and I will pay him back for the wrongs he did me." That is why he teaches true righteousness: what is truly just is to render to each his own. "First, honor the Lord from your just labors, and give him the firstfruits of your fruits of righteousness." Then: "Honor the king," and render what is due to your parents, and what is equal to everyone. This is one form of righteousness. The second is to make one's own soul righteous and keep it in balance, so that it does not tip into imbalance. As regards the reasoning part: "Let no evil counsel overtake you, which forsakes the teaching of youth; but do all things with counsel, and let your thoughts be judgments." So each person judges himself, and every desire he has is good, for every desire of the righteous is good, and the desire of the righteous is acceptable. As regards the spirited part: "Do not be a companion to a hot-tempered man, and do not lodge with an angry friend. For a fool vents all his anger, but the wise man doles it out little by little." A man who orders himself in this way, and keeps the proper activity of each part of his soul sound and unharmed, will know true righteousness. "Directing judgments" means, first, judging justly according to the law of God, as it says: "Open your mouth with the word of God, and judge all soundly. Give judgment for the poor and the weak. For whoever says to the ungodly, You are righteous, will be cursed by peoples and hated by nations. For it is not good to show partiality in judgment." This is to be said in the plain sense. But it also means that the judgment one passes on others should be directed toward oneself as well. One should test oneself: rebuking oneself if anger gets the upper hand, restraining oneself if desire overflows, and rousing oneself if the reasoning part dozes off, saying: "How long will you lie there, sluggard?" By leading himself justly in this way and becoming his own accuser, he will learn to direct judgment, and he will not hear from another: "You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who say, Do not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?" For just as one who walks and keeps his road straight arrives at the end, so one who directs judgments will be known as just and wise. Parables are words that serve as images of what is being said, for through them, by the likeness, what is said is grasped. This is how the Lord spoke, as Mark says: "To what shall I liken the kingdom of God? Or with what parable shall I compare it?" For what is said by way of likeness is a parable. Indeed, after saying, "The kingdom of God is like," he later added:

"That is why I speak to them in parables." Parables, then, are like these: "As snow falling at harvest is a help against the heat, so a faithful messenger helps those who sent him"; and again: "Like winds and clouds and rains are those who boast of a false gift"; and the like. Sayings of the wise are words that are not sophistical and do not deceive by plausibility, but are exact. They are not spoken as commands, but as things the wise have come to know for themselves, and they are put forward as their own conclusions. Examples are: "When the heart is glad, the face flourishes, but when it is in sorrow, it is downcast"; and: "An upright heart seeks understanding, but the mouth of the uninstructed will know evils"; and: "Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all who are not contentious"; and: "Whoever despises a matter will be despised by it, but whoever fears a commandment is healthy." The words of other men are for the most part ambiguous, but those of the wise, such as these, are true and exact on every side, so that they cannot be contradicted. Other men recognize a thing from the end result of an action: for example, that the unjust man is base and the adulterer wicked. That would be plain to anyone. But the wise foretell the beginnings of actions, and announce in advance, like signs, the movements of the soul, so that each person, knowing the beginnings of evils, may be on guard. Such are the words already quoted: "Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all who are not contentious." For the lover of strife has the beginning of this kind of wickedness in hatred, and no one would say that the contentious man loves. Conversely, the man who is not contentious bears a mark of love, and no one would call a loving man contentious. Likewise this saying: "Every idle man is full of desires, and the hot-tempered man acts thoughtlessly." Here he indicated that the soul of the idle man is sunk in every kind of desire, and showed that the hot-tempered man has not a single sound counsel. In general, these sayings are mainly concerned with conduct, and tell us where an action takes its beginning. Hatred comes before contentiousness, and love before freedom from contention. Wicked pleasure comes before idleness, and thoughtlessness before hot temper. The beginning of being despised is despising the law oneself, while the fear of God comes before health. The beginning of the soul's destruction is an unguarded mouth, and rashness comes before terror. If you analyze each saying in this way, you will find that it was spoken and written so that its hearers, learning the beginnings of evil and of good, may flee what is base and do what is good. Riddles and dark words are those that are so obscure [?] that they frustrate the reader, because they reveal nothing and offer no hint. Yet when they are searched out, they disclose the meaning within them. Examples are: "The leech has three daughters

…were loved with love [?]; and these three, and the fourth was not satisfied to say, “Enough”: Hades, and the love of a woman, and Tartarus, and earth that is not filled with water, and water and fire will never say, “It is enough.”” And again: “Three things are impossible for me to understand, and the fourth I do not know: the tracks of an eagle in flight, and the ways of a serpent on a rock, and the paths of a ship crossing the sea, and the ways of a man in his youth.” The same goes for all other riddles of this kind. They point to one thing and bring something else to mind. They are obscure, but they hold a hidden meaning.

Book 15: Ecclesiastes. 25. Solomon also wrote this book, as was said before. It is called Ecclesiastes because its author gave himself this name, saying at the beginning: “The words of the Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Israel in Jerusalem: Vanity of vanities, said the Ecclesiastes.” Solomon could be called by various names: wise, because he had a share in wisdom; prudent, because the prudence of truth was in him; instructed, because he had received true instruction from the Lord. He was called Ecclesiastes, then, because he gathered the peoples into assembly and spoke the things of the Spirit. In this book he can be seen philosophizing about the contemplation of nature. The Egyptians were indulging their fancies about these things, and the Greeks were going to make myths about them. So he, moved by the Holy Spirit, puts a stop to those who try to inquire into them, saying: “Man will not be able to find out the work that is done under the sun; however much a man may toil to seek it, he will not find it.” He also discredits the Egyptians' notion of casting nativities, saying: “He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who looks at the clouds will not reap. Among these there is no one who knows what the way of the wind is. As with the bones in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you will not know the works of God, all that he will make.” Then, after examining each of these things, he saw that it is vain to inquire into such matters, and that they only produce toil. For a wise and righteous man is not made by knowing such things but by the practical life. He says: “And indeed, whatever the wise man says he will come to know, he will not be able to find it. For I gave all this to my heart, and my soul saw all this: that the righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God.” So he rightly moves beyond the inquiry into such things and turns to the way people live. Seeing the many and various things that befall them, he shows that all things are governed by providence, saying: “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the intelligent [the mighty], nor indeed bread to the wise,

nor indeed wealth to the intelligent, nor indeed favour to those who have knowledge; for time and chance will meet them all.” “For in everything there is a king of the cultivated field.” For in these matters, he says, no one is master of his own counsel. “For who is the man who will follow after counsel, in all that he has done?” He also teaches that in this life a man has no greater power than to do evil or good and to prepare his works for his departure. Indeed, even what he eats and drinks is a gift of God. So whether it is the inquiry into how the visible world came to be, or the acquisition of money, or the luxury of wealth, all these are vanity of vanities. They are nothing more than an excess of counsel and an exertion of the will. But in calling these things vanity, he points to the eternity of the things to come. So, passing over everything, he urges us to remember the eternal things and to know that this world will have an end. He says this when he speaks of the grinding women falling idle: “in the day when the keepers of the house are shaken, and the men of strength are perverted, and the grinding women have ceased.” He also explains what comes after the end: “For God will bring every work into judgment, with everything overlooked, whether it is good or whether it is evil.” From this he shows that when he said “Vanity of vanities,” he was not disparaging creation. Rather, because he was contemplating eternal things, he was saying that the desire for temporary things is vanity. And by teaching about judgment he points to the resurrection of the dead and the repayment of deeds. Then, by saying “The grinding women have ceased,” he shows again that creation itself is not vain. On the contrary, it is a teacher to all, leading them to piety. For its order and arrangement tell of the one who made and created it. Within it the prophets, the evangelists and the teachers are like women grinding at the mill: through their teaching they grind for each person the food of knowledge that leads to piety. And these grinders will then cease at the consummation. For they will no longer teach like women grinding at the mill; rather, the judgment will be based on the deeds of each

Book 16: The Song of Songs. 24. This book too is a composition of Solomon, as was shown before. He wrote all of it, from beginning to end, in a mystical way, using enigmatic allegory. The meaning of its teachings is hidden, not in what is plain to see but in what is secret. It is found when one searches it out. That is why the intelligent should read the whole of it allegorically, so that what it says may not fall into dishonour through the ignorance of the unlearned. It is called the Song of Songs because it comes after the other songs, and after it there is no other to be expected. By “other” I do not mean another book but what the book signifies. What I mean is this: all of divine Scripture prophesies about the descent of the Word to us and his presence in the flesh. For this is the purpose [?] Eccl. 9 [?]

of God. This was the chief thing that the prophets and all of divine Scripture had to proclaim. Alongside this divine account, they also speak about the nations: Babylon, Damascus, Moab [?] and the rest. Throughout each book of Scripture they rebuke sinners and urge those who have been overtaken by sin to repent, threatening the coming judgment of fire. The other Scriptures foretell him. Moses says: “The Lord our God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me.” Isaiah says: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son.” Micah says: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest.” And each of the others foretells him in his own way, according to the grace of the Spirit. While all of them were speaking, the Lord whom they announced was being awaited. That is why many announced him, and the prophets did not cease until he came. All of these are songs. But the Song of Songs does not prophesy or foreshadow. It shows the one whom the others announced beforehand as having already come and already taken on flesh. That is why the Song of Songs sings a wedding song, as for the marriage of the Word and the flesh. The other Scriptures speak about the Saviour, but in between they also deal with other matters. This book sings only of the union of the Word with the body. So in the other Scriptures, because of the matters treated in between, there are words of wrath and anger and threats of terrors. But this book signifies nothing other than the presence of the Word alone, and so its words are of gladness, joy and delight only. For when the bridegroom is present, all should rejoice and no one should mourn, as the Lord himself said. When he was present he bore our infirmities and turned our griefs into joy. After the Saviour's dispensation we no longer expect a prophet. In the same way, after what is signified in the Song of Songs we can expect nothing newer to be signified. For what is signified in the Song is also found in the prophets and in the other Scriptures, spoken at intervals. Again: when John pointed out the Lamb, the law and the prophets lasted until John. In the same way, what is signified in the Song of Songs is the fulfilment of everything signified in all of divine Scripture. For after the coming of Christ, what else are we to expect but judgment and recompense? That is why the Phrygian sect, who bring in prophets after the Lord, are in error and were condemned as heretics. It is called the Song of Songs, then, because after what it signifies nothing else is to be expected. Under the law there was the Holy Place, and after the Holy Place the Holy of Holies, and beyond the Holy of Holies there was no more inner place. In the same way, after the songs comes the Song of Songs, and after the Song of Songs we can expect no further inner or newer promise. For once and for all the Word became flesh and completed the work. This whole book is full of dialogues:

of the old people with the Word; of the human race as a whole with the Word; of the Church from the Gentiles with him; and of the Word in turn with her and with the human race. Then there is a dialogue of the Gentiles with Jerusalem, and of Jerusalem about the Church from the Gentiles and about herself. Then there is also the proclamation of the ministering angels to the people who have been called. So the old people, begging him to come down and be joined to flesh, says this: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine.” And again it urges him with these words: “New things along with old I have kept for you, my beloved.” And all together say to the Word, asking him to take on our body: “Who will grant you to me, my beloved, as one nursing at my mother's breasts? Finding you outside, I will kiss you, and they will not despise me. I will take you and bring you into my mother's house, into the chamber of her who conceived me.” For they were asking him to take on a body not from outside but from the womb from which we were born, though not, as we are, from a man and a woman. For as creator he took the body for himself from a virgin alone, yet still from a human being, for Mary the Theotokos was human. And to those who had asked, the Word, now taking on flesh from the Virgin, says this: “I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my bread with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.” For he entered his own garden, creation, took to himself the body from the Virgin, and became man. The body was mortal, but it was joined with the fragrance of the all-holy Word. And if, as a man, he let the body take milk, he also gave it a share in the wine of his own perfection. For just as he took milk, so in that same body he performed the works of the Godhead. Then the Word, having put on the body, calls the old people, as the first to be entrusted with the oracles, in these words: “Arise, come near me, my fair one, my dove; for behold, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared in the land, the time of pruning has come, the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land, the fig tree has put forth its green figs, our vines are in blossom.” He teaches the first people as one that had received the shadow in the law for a time, and he reminds it as one that knew the voice of the turtledove. Having called Jerusalem, the Word then also calls those from the Gentiles (for there is one Lord of both Jews and Gentiles) in these words: “Come from Lebanon, my bride. From Lebanon you will come, and you will pass on from the beginning of faith, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards.” For he calls her to faith out of idolatry and a bestial way of life. So she, called from among the Gentiles and already pierced to the heart, says this to the Word: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where do you pasture your flock, where do you make it rest at noon? Lest I become like one who is veiled beside the flocks of your companions.”

Since she knew from experience what it was to turn from one thing to many others, she asked to be established and confirmed from then on, so that the same thing would not happen to her again. At her entreaty the Word then teaches her in these words: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out in the footsteps of the flocks, and pasture your kids beside the shepherds' tents.” For no one can know God without first knowing himself. Piety toward God is the beginning of perception, and that perception is not outward but the understanding of the soul joined with faith. Jerusalem, seeing the calling of the Gentiles take place in the uncircumcision of faith, says in wonder: “What will you see in the Shulammite, who comes like dancers from the camps?” For they came not from one nation but from every nation, leaving their own camps, breaking their swords, and from then on minded for peace. The Church from the Gentiles, seeing that Jerusalem seems to find fault with her, defends herself, saying that her calling is not in vain: “I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. Do not look at me because I am darkened, because the sun has looked upon me. My mother's sons fought against me; they made me keeper of the vineyards. My own vineyard I have not kept.” I am black, but I am under the sun itself. For even if I am uncircumcised, she says, I have renounced idols and gone out from my mother's house, just as Abraham did; for I belong to his faith. And that is why I ask: “Bring me into the house of wine, set love upon me, keep me with perfumes, sustain me with apples, for I am wounded with love.” Do not look at my uncircumcision, but receive me in love, O law and prophets. And if I smell foul from my wildness, instruct me yourself and strengthen me with your fragrance, for I am wounded with love. And that is why: “I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, that you do not rouse or awaken love until it pleases.” I adjure you, O fathers, not by the powers, for that is not lawful, but by the powers of paradise, so that, looking to it, you may receive me as you would Adam. For there too there was no circumcision, and now the things of Adam are being renewed. The Word, seeing the faith of the Gentiles and accepting it, says: “You are beautiful, my companion, like good pleasure, lovely as Jerusalem, awe-inspiring as armies in array.” For those from the Gentiles must be nothing other than like Jerusalem, so that they may become one people. This happens when we believe in Christ while also honouring the law. For the God of the law and of the Gospels is one. And whoever does not become like Jerusalem does not come near the Word. Jerusalem, seeing the faith of the children and the Word's love for humanity, says: “I went down into the walnut garden to see the produce of the brook, whether the pomegranates had blossomed; there I will give you my breasts. My soul did not know; it set me as the chariots of Amminadab.” For I came into the walnut garden, that is, into the Scriptures, which are like walnuts: hard on the outside

but spiritual within. I saw that I must be yoked, as in a chariot, with the calling of the Gentiles. So when both peoples had been yoked together, the proclamation was sent out everywhere, and the angels became its ministers, saying: “Go out and see King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.” For whoever goes out from wickedness will also see the unchangeable union of the Word with the body. When the Word's marriage with us took place through his union with the body, he also won the victory over death, and through it he filled all things with gladness. Such are the dialogues in the Song of Songs. Taking them as a starting point, one can match like with like according to their sense, from the book itself.

Book 17: Job. 25. The book is titled Job because it contains his story. It tells how he suffered when the devil tested him, and how, having overcome and piously endured the blows brought upon him, he received everything back double. He became more glorious than he had been before and again had ten children. He suffered when he was seventy years old, so that his whole life came to two hundred and forty years, for after the blows he lived another hundred and seventy years. Job lived before Moses. He was fifth in line from Abraham, a descendant of Esau. Because of the blow that had struck him, three of his friends came to comfort him: Eliphaz, king of the Temanites; Bildad, ruler of the Shuhites; and Zophar, king of the Minaeans. They spoke to him contentiously and without mercy, attacking him, so that it was even reckoned to them as a sin. But Job interceded with God for them, and they were forgiven. Job has nine speeches to his friends. Eliphaz has three speeches to him, Zophar two, and Bildad three. There is also one by Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite. Finally the Lord speaks to Job through the whirlwind and the clouds, and Job answers the Lord twice.

Book 18: The Twelve Prophets. Hosea, 1. 26. There were prophets even before him. In the time of David there were Samuel, Nathan and Gad. In the time of Rehoboam, Abijah and Asa there were Ahijah the Shilonite, Shemaiah, Iddo, Azariah and Hanani. In the time of Jehoshaphat and Ahab there were Elijah and Elisha; the prophet who prophesied to Ahab about Syria; the one who struck himself with a wound and rebuked Ahab; Jehu son of Hanani; Jahaziel [?]; and Eliezer [?]. But no writings of their own survive, only their words recorded in Kings and Chronicles. Of those who wrote and whose writings survive, the first were

these: Hosea and Isaiah. For they prophesied under the same kings: under the kings of Judah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. The word came to Hosea, and he prophesies against¹ the priests, against Israel and against the king's house, and about the destruction of Samaria. Having rebuked them and shut them up in disobedience, he points to the Church from the Gentiles. For this reason [?] he himself took a harlot for a wife; and having taken her, he brought her to chastity and led her back to himself. He also prophesies about the coming of the Saviour.

As we said before, he and Hosea were contemporaries, since he too lived under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. He saw a vision and prophesies against Judea and against Jerusalem, and the word of the Lord came to him. Most of his prophecy is good news about the coming of the Word of God in the flesh, and about the sufferings he took on himself for our sake. He also prophesies against these nations: against Babylon, against the Philistines, against Damascus. He gives a vision of Egypt, a vision of Idumea, a vision of the valley of Zion, a vision of Tyre, and a vision of the four-footed beasts in the desert. He also tells of Sennacherib's expedition and Rabshakeh's arrogance, and of their fall and destruction. He tells how Hezekiah fell ill and was about to die, but prayed and was granted fifteen more years of life. He also prophesies to eunuchs and to the Gentiles, and at the end about the day of judgment. Book 20. Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, of the priests. 39. As we said before, he and Zephaniah were contemporaries. Jeremiah lived on until Jehoiakim, and until the eleventh year of Zedekiah king of Judah, up to the captivity of the people. The word of God came to him, the word of the Lord that came to him. The word of the Lord came to him many times, and in many ways he rebukes the iniquities of Jerusalem. He prophesies against Jerusalem, about the drought, and against the nations: against Elam; about the king of Babylon coming to strike the land of Egypt; and against Babylon. There is also the word that the Lord commanded Jeremiah to speak to Seraiah son of Neriah. He speaks to Idumea, to the sons of Ammon, to Kedar and the queen of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck, to Damascus and to Moab, and against Jerusalem and Judah. He speaks to the house of the Rechabites about the sons of Jonadab, and to the Jews who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes and in the land of Pathros. He speaks also to Baruch, when Baruch wrote these words in the book from Jeremiah's dictation. Toward the end the book tells how the Jews plotted against the prophet and threw him into a muddy cistern, and how Ebed-melech the Ethiopian brought him up.

The book is titled Baruch because Baruch wrote down from Jeremiah's dictation the words in the book and read them to those taken captive to Babylon. He comforted them and promised them the hope that comes from God. The book is titled Lamentations because Jeremiah lamented over Jerusalem in these words when the city was taken and the people carried off captive. It is called the Letter of Jeremiah because Jeremiah wrote it to those in captivity to guard them against idols, so that when they saw the idols they would not be led astray along with those who worship them. Book 21. Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest. 40. He lived in the captivity after Jeremiah, and he began to prophesy in the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity. The word of the Lord came to him, and the hand of the Lord came upon him. At the beginning he sees a vision of a four-faced living creature, marvelous, most astonishing and hard to interpret. He prophesies against the prophets of Israel. He speaks about the wood of the vine and tells an allegory about the eagle. He testifies against Jerusalem, setting out its iniquities and sins. He speaks about the proverb they used to quote: "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth were set on edge." He speaks to the sons of Ammon and about Oholah and Oholibah. He raises a lament over Tyre and speaks against Sidon, about the day of the Lord, and to Pharaoh king of Egypt. He raises a lament over Pharaoh and Egypt, and speaks against Mount Seir, about the bones that came back to life, and against Gog and the land of Magog. He speaks to the ruler of Tyre and raises a lament against him, and speaks to the sons of his people and against the shepherds of Israel. Finally he prophesies, describing the building of the temple and of Jerusalem. Book 22. Daniel. 41. He too lived in the captivity, until Cyrus king of Persia. He himself judges the case of Susanna and condemns the elders as false accusers. He also tells the king's dreams and interprets them. He sees complete visions as well: two about the kingdoms, and two about the coming of the Savior, the end of Jerusalem and the coming of the Antichrist. He tells of the martyrdom of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego and of their hymn. They were saved, while those who stoked the furnace were burned up, and the king repented. He also tells how he himself was twice thrown into the lions' den. The first time was because, while the Babylonians were praying to King Darius, he alone prayed to God. The second time was because he overthrew Bel and killed the dragon under King Cyrus. He was saved and came up out of the den, away from the lions, but those who had plotted against him were thrown into the lions' den and immediately devoured by

Here end the canonical books of the Old Testament, which total twenty-two, the same as the number of letters among the Hebrews. As we said before, that is how many letters they have. Next we must speak in the same way about the other books of the Old Testament, which are not canonical but are only read, as was explained earlier. Book: Esther. 42. The book is called this because it contains the story of Esther. It tells how the Jews were about to be destroyed with their whole race, and how God saved them through her and struck down Haman, who had set out to plot against them. The story took place in Susa, and it goes like this. King Artaxerxes put away his own wife and searched his kingdom for the most beautiful and lovely woman of all, to take [?] as his wife. Esther was found, and she happened to be Jewish by race. Mordecai, her kinsman, was also in that same country, from the captivity that took place under Zedekiah. The king made one of his men, named Haman, great and ordered everyone to bow down to him. But Mordecai would not bow down to him, because of his worship of God. Haman was enraged, and when he learned that Mordecai was a Jew, he persuaded King Artaxerxes and wrote an order that all the Jews in his kingdom were to be destroyed root and branch on a single day in the twelfth month. When Mordecai learned this he mourned, and while fasting he threw himself at Esther's feet and begged her for help. Esther fasted and prayed to God, then adorned herself in royal attire. She had not been summoned, and no one was permitted to enter unsummoned. Even so she went in to the king out of turn, trusting in prayer instead of the proper time. The king was amazed at this unusual thing, and she collapsed from fear. But God changed the king's anger into goodwill and gentleness. He rose, lifted the woman up and urged her not to be afraid, and he even invited her to ask for whatever she wished. She asked the king himself and Haman to come to a banquet, not once but a second time. Haman was elated and delighted at being thought worthy of an invitation from the queen, and he grew even more arrogant toward Mordecai. He had a great gallows cut, and he meant to hang Mordecai on it the next day. But by some good providence the king lay awake that night. Unable to sleep, he ordered the records of his reign to be read to him. As they were read, he found a good deed that Mordecai had done for him: two eunuchs had been about to plot against the king, and Mordecai had reported them to the king himself and exposed them. The king approved of Mordecai's loyalty and looked for a fitting honor to give such a man. When Haman came in to him early in the morning, the king asked him what kind of honor, and how great, was due to someone who had done the king a good service. Haman thought the king was asking about him and said it was right for

[?] such a man to be called second to the king. So the king ordered that Mordecai be given this honor and that Haman walk before him. Esther found her opportunity and pleaded for the Jews. The king was grieved at the lawless decree against the Jews and angry with Haman. While the king was away, Haman himself pleaded with Esther, bending down and clasping her knees in supplication. The king came in and saw Haman holding the queen's knees. Suspecting that he was doing this with shameful intent, he ordered Haman to be hanged on the gallows Haman had prepared for Mordecai. He then wrote that all the Jews were to have relief and that their enemies were to be killed by them. The Jews killed fifteen thousand people. Because of this, a festival was established for them on the fourteenth and fifteenth of the twelfth month, which is called Adar. In their own language this day is called Phroure. That is why on this day the Jews burn Haman and hold a festival, since it is a memorial of their deliverance. Book: Judith. 43. The book is called this because it contains the story of Judith. It tells how the sons of Israel were under attack and besieged by Holofernes, and how God saved the people through her and struck down Holofernes. The story goes like this. Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians was at war with Arphaxad king of the Medes. He asked all the nations as far as Egypt to fight alongside him. None of them sent help; they all refused. After he had defeated Arphaxad and gained the upper hand, he declared war on those who had refused and sent Holofernes against them with a great army. Holofernes conquered all the other nations and smashed their idols. But the sons of Israel fortified themselves and would not submit to Holofernes, nor were they afraid of his threats. Joakim the priest wrote to the people of Bethulia telling them to block Holofernes' road, since his route ran through there, and they blocked it. Holofernes drew up his army for battle. But Achior, the leader of the sons of Ammon, advised Holofernes not to make war on the nation of the Hebrews, because God protects them. Holofernes was enraged and sent him to Bethulia, threatening to kill him once he had defeated the Hebrews. So Achior stayed in Bethulia, while Holofernes besieged the city, having first seized its water supply. The people were already fainting from thirst, and the rulers were about to surrender the city. Then Judith put off her widow's clothes (she was mourning her husband and fasted continually) and adorned herself like a bride. She urged the rulers earnestly not to surrender the city for five days. Then she went out to Holofernes herself, deceived him by her wisdom, and on the

third day cut off his head without his soldiers knowing. So the Assyrians fled, and the sons of Israel ran together from every side and cut them down. Having been saved in this way, they plundered the enemy and gave Judith everything that had belonged to Holofernes. Judith herself went to Jerusalem and dedicated it all to the Lord. Then she returned home and kept up the same discipline as before. She remained a widow until her death, since no one could persuade her to marry. She lived her widowhood well and died at the age of one hundred and five. Book: Tobit. 44. The book is called this because it contains the story of Tobit himself. He was of the tribe of Naphtali. He lived during the captivity, in Nineveh, and was merciful and devout. Even in captivity he did not eat the common bread of the Gentiles but kept himself pure. He was also purchasing agent for King Enemessar, and he deposited ten talents with Gabael in Media. This Tobit was zealous in burying Jews who died. He was denounced to King Achirel and fled. After he came back, he buried one of the dead and slept outside the wall. As was his habit, he slept with his eyes open; white films formed over them, and he could no longer see. In Ecbatana there was a daughter of his kinsman Raguel, named Sarah. The demon Asmodeus would not let her be married, and he killed seven men in turn who took her as wife. The girl was deeply grieved and prayed, and God sent her a helper, the archangel Raphael. Tobit charged his son Tobias not to take a wife from anywhere else but from his own tribe and family. He gave him the bond for the ten talents and told him to go and claim the money. The boy did not know the road or the man, so he went out to look for a travel companion. By God's providence he found Raphael standing outside in the form of a man, and hired him, since Raphael said he knew the road. So the angel traveled with him as a man, under the name Azariah. When they came to the river Tigris, the boy wanted to go down into it and wash, and at once a large fish leapt at the lad. The angel told him to catch the fish, cut it open, take out the liver, the heart and the gall, and keep them. When the boy asked, "What are these good for?" the angel said, "When the liver and the heart are burned as incense, they will drive away the demon, and the gall will clear away the white films." So with his counsel and help the boy took Raguel's daughter Sarah as his wife. The demon was driven off by this incense and bound by the angel in the upper parts of Egypt. Tobias stayed with his wife and sent Azariah to Media, as though he were a man. Azariah claimed the ten talents, and Tobias returned with his wife and with him to his father. When the boy got back, he anointed

his father's eyes with the fish's gall. The scales fell off, and at once his father could see. Tobit was fifty-eight years old when he was blinded and sixty-six when he regained his sight. Once he could see, the angel revealed that he was not a man but had been sent from God to help them and Sarah. When Tobit had grown old, he charged his son Tobias to go away to Media because of the coming overthrow of Nineveh, as the prophet Jonah had foretold. Then his strength failed and he died at the age of one hundred and fifty-eight. His son Tobias went to Media, buried his parents-in-law, heard of the overthrow of Nineveh, and died

Book: Wisdom of Solomon. 45. The book is called the Wisdom of Solomon, since they say Solomon wrote this one too. It contains teaching about righteousness and about how to tell worthless men from good ones, along with prophecy about Christ. It teaches that wisdom is gained through much toil and longing. It also contains some natural philosophy. It speaks against idols, against those who carve them, and against those who put their hope in them and worship them. It also contains a hymn of thanksgiving for the wonders God worked for the Israelites in the sight of their enemies. That is the general content of the book; the summary runs as follows. In the opening there is an exhortation to the righteous to be godly, and a refutation of the blasphemous ungodly. "Do not envy," it says, "the antichrists, who are death." It shows how the ungodly came to crucify the Lord of glory, because they preferred this present age. It shows that they also persecuted and killed the apostles. Some will despise the law of the Lord, and some will submit to it. God will not spare the ungodly who sin against Christ, however many they are, for God cares for even one righteous person who believes in Christ, even if he dies young. "For honorable old age is not a matter of length of time." And even if the ungodly despised the death of the one who believes in Christ, such people are still chosen by Christ. The ungodly will be handed over to a dishonorable fall. Those who persecute Christ's servants will be cast down in a great judgment, and at the judgment they will see his glory and the glory of his servants, and see themselves headed for punishment. It shows that wealth joined with arrogance has done us no good. It shows what the wrath is against those who act ungodly toward Christ. It exhorts the rulers of Israel to believe in Christ. More precisely, it instructs the rulers of the Catholic Church in how they must rule now that Israel has turned away. It shows what wisdom is: the Son of God. It shows how the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. "I too am a man, subject to the same sufferings as you, and I have been taught by God's command." It speaks about Christ, the wisdom of God. "I received the knowledge of all things from her, for both we and our words are in his hand." It shows what wisdom is and how she came to human beings: though she is one, she can do all things, and while remaining in herself she renews all things. "The [?]

"Wisdom," he says, "I loved from my youth, and from her I received every good thing," both bodily and spiritual. That, having come to know the greatness of wisdom, he appealed to the Lord that the Holy Spirit might be given to him to enlighten him about her, and she was sent to labour alongside him. "For the reasonings of mortals are timid." On the works of wisdom: how she guarded the first-formed man; from how many evils God saves those who believe in him, and how many good things he provides, as with Noah, Abraham, Lot, Jacob, Joseph, and the Israelites, whom he rescued from the hand of the Egyptians through Moses, and to whom water was given out of the flinty rock. How he sent hornets against the seven nations. Yet, exercising long-suffering, he gave even these room for repentance, teaching the people through them to be humane. Against worshippers of the elements: frogs, gnats, mice, locusts, hornets, snakes. Against idolaters, for idols made of gold and silver, or of stone, or of wood. That there is also salvation through wood for those who believe. On those who make idols or paint them. On all the evils found in idolatry. On impious worship and all the evils in it. On the potter, and the clay idols of the Gentiles' worship. On the most hateful animals, snakes, cats and the like. That God blessed Israel with quail in place of frogs. That even against the bite of snakes there was salvation for the people through a bronze serpent raised up as on a cross; but he slew their enemies with locusts and mice. That he fed the people with the food of angels, able to give every delight and suited to every taste. That he sent hail mixed with fire upon the Egyptians to destroy their crops. That he sent upon the Egyptians a darkness that could be felt, and the evils it brought; but to his holy ones he gave light in Egypt, and in the wilderness a pillar of fire. And in return for the death of Israel's infants came the death of the Egyptians' firstborn and their drowning; and in place of the death of the firstborn, the salvation of Israel through the blood of a lamb. And when the righteous were dying in the wilderness, Aaron made atonement, praying to the Lord and offering incense; but when the Egyptians were dying in the Red Sea, there was merciless wrath, while for the people there was a marvellous passage. That the Egyptians suffered these things because of their hatred of strangers, as did the Sodomites. That the elements are subject to the divine judgment of Christ, being tuned to whatever he wills, as the strings of a lyre are to the lyre-player. In these lies the whole substance of the Wisdom of Solomon, called the All-Virtuous. The Book of the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach. 46. This Jesus was the son of Sirach and the grandson of

a Jesus of the same name. He lived, then, in later times, after the captivity and the return, and after all the prophets. Now his grandfather Jesus, as he himself testifies, was a diligent and most prudent man, who not only collected the sayings of other wise men before him but also uttered some of his own, full of great wisdom and understanding. When, then, the first Jesus departed from among men leaving this book behind, Sirach his son received it after him and in turn left it to his own son Jesus. He took it up, made the whole into a single harmonious compilation, and gave it the title Wisdom, after his own name and those of his father and his grandfather, intending by the very name of wisdom to draw the hearer more lovingly to the study of the book. It contains, then, words of prudence, riddles and parables, and certain particular ancient histories dear to God, about men who pleased God, together with their prayer and hymn; and further, the benefits God granted to his people, and the evils with which he filled their enemies. This Jesus, then, being a follower of Solomon, excelled no less than he in wisdom and learning, being both truly and by name a man of great learning. Such, as one might say, is the scope of the book. Its summary should be understood as follows. In the opening it speaks of all the wisdom of the Lord; then of anger, of fear and of fearlessness; of the knowledge of wisdom; of the fear of God; of the need to approach God without hypocrisy; of temptations and endurance; of cowardice and faintheartedness; of love for the Lord; of honour toward parents; of the meekness and gentleness of the humble; of rash and unruly inquiry into things not commanded; of the hard-hearted and proud man; of the wise and teachable man; of the merciful man and the protection [?] of orphans; toward a submissive and gentle friend; of the exaltation of the sons of wisdom; of the insubordination of the wicked; and of shame, both harmful and beneficial; not to put words before deeds, nor to become a self-appointed teacher. Of not being bound by the craving for money, nor supposing that one sins with impunity, even if we do not pay the penalty at once, for God is long-suffering; and that one must propitiate him, and not walk in the desire of one's heart. Of not being carried about by every wind, and of idle talk and arrogance; of the lover of pleasure; the testing of the faithful and the unfaithful; of the discipline of the Lord, that one must desire it from youth to old age; of unprofitable listening; of not betraying a friend, nor missing the chance of a wise wife; of servants, of possessions; of children; of women; of not doing evil, nor loving power, nor making light of sin. Of not lying to a brother, nor babbling in the presence of elders, nor repeating a word; of the glory of a father

or a mother, and of piety toward God, and honour toward priests, and visiting the afflicted. That in every matter one must foresee the end and only then begin; in every word or deed one must consider the outcome. And of not neglecting the discourse of wise old men. From how many things fornication arises; of not abandoning an old friend, for a new friend is like new wine; of the wise craftsman, the judge and teacher, and the uneducated king. That the physician watches over a long illness; of honourable and faithless offspring; of the wise servant and the rich ruler. That the bee is small among winged creatures, yet its fruit is the chief of sweet things. Of not blaming without judgment or inquiry, nor being a busybody, but being just, for it is God who makes rich. That one should consider none of the goods of this life secure. Of not being intimate with everyone, but with the pious and just; and of guarding against the wicked. Of not associating with the proud, because of the defilement and ruin that come from it; and of the courting of one's neighbour by many; and that every creature loves its like. For as a wolf has no fellowship with a lamb, nor a hyena peace with a dog, so neither has a sinner with a pious man. Of misers who do not share with others, and that in wealth and in poverty alike one should be just and holy, not the reverse. To count blessed the one who lives with wisdom and understanding until his end, not the one who is rich in the world. Of free will: that you should not blame the Lord for falling away, for he has set everything before you. That it is better to be childless than to have wicked children. That nothing escapes God. Of God's detection and judgment, and not to think that the lawless are hidden from God or escape his judgment. Of created things. Of the fashioning of man, and the honour bestowed on him. Of the giving of the law; of almsgiving and repentance; of a gentle answer; of not finding fault with a good deed, nor giving a gift with a hurtful word; that whoever wishes to begin something should look ahead [?] and prepare beforehand in all things. Of not living prodigally, and of what one must abstain from. Of keeping secrets, and of the fool; of wisdom conveyed through parables; and of life, rule, the wise and the foolish. Of a bold daughter; and of the fool's heedlessness; and of a steadfast mind, and what things dissolve friendship; and of not speaking unguardedly to those who have sinned. Of discipline, and of not demanding an oath; of guarding soul and body, and of the fornicating man. Of the wicked woman and the adulteress. A prophecy about Jesus Christ, who is Wisdom and Son, likened to rivers. Of increase in instruction; of the ten beatitudes; of the infliction of blows and vengeance; of a merchant's wrongdoing; of those who reveal a secret word. Of the hot-tempered man; of the talkative man; of lending to one's neighbour and not taking interest, but

lending to him when he is in need; of standing surety for one's neighbour; and of life; of not [?] in turning to discipline children; of the health of body, of food, and of the soul; of instruction concerning wealth, great men and rulers; [?] to son and wife, brother and friend; of a wicked servant. Of senseless dreams; of wandering and wide experience; and of those who fear the Lord. Of sacrifices and offerings that come from injustice, and offerings that come from righteousness; of sacrifices that come from love of money. That one must despise luxury and wealth. Of the gluttonous, the envious, the insatiable and the disorderly; not to get drunk with wine, but to use it in moderation. Of the gentle man who is exalted [?]; and of the speech of elders, and of the speech of a young man. Of receiving the instruction of the law, its judgments and ordinances, and of trusting the law. Of God's covenant from generation to generation; and that the constitution of nature is one and the same for all people, but their choice differs, on account of which he made some blessed and put others under a curse. Of the chosen people; and that evil stands opposite good, and the sinner opposite the pious. With whom one should associate; what sort of wife one should take; what sort of friends one should have; what counsellors one should use; what teachers one should appoint; of each knowing what is beneficial. Of honouring physicians. How one should mourn for the dead. Of the scribe and the wise farmer; and of the wakefulness of the carpenter, the smith and the potter. Of guarding a man's soul, and of the wisdom that abides, and how much it attains. Of God's foreknowledge and the creation of the world. That creation turns to blessing for the pious, but to a curse for the lawless. That great toil has been created for every man, and a heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam. That all things that come from the earth return to the earth, and all that come from the waters return to the sea. Of a comparison of goods, and which are the lesser, bodily goods. Of which are the greater and spiritual goods. Of a life of begging. Of the bitter death of the rich man; of the good death of the poor man. Of not fearing to die. Of not living disgracefully, but caring for a good name. Of instruction in peace. What one ought to be ashamed of; what one ought not to be ashamed of. That one must always be anxious about a virgin daughter; of not sitting in the midst of women, because of fornication. Of the Lord's creation. Of the sun, that it is a marvellous instrument and a work of the Lord. Of the moon and the stars, and the rainbow, and snows, and lightnings. Of clouds and hail. Of earthquakes and thunder. Of rain, frost and mist. Of dew after scorching heat, and of the dry deep. Of the Jordan and the sea. Of every living creature and beast. Of the glorious creation of the Lord. Of his benefits. Epilogue on Enoch and Noah. Epilogue on Abraham and Isaac, and how they were tested. Epilogue on Jacob and

Moses, and the wonders he worked. Epilogue on Aaron, his ministry and his priesthood. Epilogue on Dathan, Abiram and Korah. Of the firstfruits of the first produce, the portion of Aaron. Epilogue: that Phinehas son of Eleazar is third in glory after Aaron. That the Lord made a covenant of kingship with David. That Joshua son of Nun becomes Moses' successor among the prophets. How in the days of Moses, Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh showed mercy, and the twelve [?] were saved. Concerning Samuel, who after Joshua judged the people among the prophets. Concerning Nathan the prophet, and a eulogy of David the king. How Solomon was wise, but later became a lover of women, and after the wrath obtained mercy through repentance. Concerning Jeroboam and Rehoboam, the authors of the schism. Concerning Elijah the prophet, the fire that burns up evils. Concerning Elisha the prophet, Elijah's disciple, who was filled with his spirit. Concerning the captivity of the kings of Judah. How Hezekiah was humble-minded, a friend of Isaiah, and the slayer of Rabshakeh. How the Lord redeemed Israel by the hand of Isaiah, striking the camp of the Assyrians. How King Josiah was a friend of Jeremiah. Of Ezekiel the prophet, that he was in the Babylonian captivity. Of the bones of the twelve prophets. How Zerubbabel and Joshua son of Jozadak built the house of the Lord. How Nehemiah raised up the fallen walls of Jerusalem. Concerning Enoch, who is among the glorious and is a support of the people. That Shem and Seth were glorious among men. That Simon son of Onias was most glorious in the high priesthood. That for all these things one must bless God who works great deeds. Against the Samaritans, who rejected Judaism, and against the Jews, who rejected Christ. Of the epilogue of the whole book. Of the prayer of Jesus son of Sirach, grandson of Jesus.

WE MUST NOW BEGIN ALSO THE BOOKS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT. 1. The Gospel according to Matthew. The book is so called because Matthew himself, the disciple of the Lord, wrote this Gospel. It narrates from the beginning the Saviour's birth according to the flesh from the seed of David. For this reason it also traces the genealogy from him down to Christ, forty-two generations. It also contains the baptism of John, the temptations by the devil on the mountain, and the great signs and wonders performed by the Saviour, the choosing of the disciples and the handing down of the mystery; and finally that he was handed over to Pilate and crucified in the body, and his body was laid in the tomb; and that the soldiers divided his garments; but he, having risen on the third day, commanded the disciples to make disciples of all the nations and to baptize them, promising to be with them all the days until the end of the age. And the signs that

Matthew relates were performed by Christ are these. The leper was cleansed; the centurion's servant was healed without being present, at his word alone; Peter's mother-in-law, sick with fever, was healed; when evening came, they brought to him those possessed by demons and those who were ill, and he cast out the spirits with a word and likewise healed the others. Christ's genealogy is given; Joseph receives the good news; the magi worship; Christ goes down into Egypt; Herod kills the children, and dies. Returning from Egypt, Christ settles in Nazareth. John comes baptizing, and turns away the Sadducees and the Pharisees. Christ is baptized and is tempted by Satan. Then, after John had been handed over, he came to Capernaum. He calls Peter and James and those with them. He heals many, sits down on the mountain and speaks the Beatitudes, and adds: "You are the salt," and, "You are the light of the world." He exhorts them about their way of life. Then he makes the commandments of the law more demanding, where he also speaks of the right eye, and of vainglory, and of love of money, and of not worrying about food, and of not judging one's neighbour. Then he says: "Do not throw your pearls before swine." An exhortation to ask; a parable on the same subject; on the narrow way, and on false prophets, and on those who keep the commandments. Here is the parable of the house built on the rock. He comes down from the mountain and heals the leper, the centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, and many others. The scribe is prevented from following, and the disciple is urged to. He stills the storm on the sea. The demons fall into the swine. Jesus came into his own city; he heals the paralytic; he calls Matthew. The Pharisees complain that he eats with tax collectors, and John's disciples that his disciples do not fast. The ruler comes to him about his little daughter, and he raises the girl; and meanwhile the woman with the haemorrhage is healed. Two blind men are healed, and a mute man possessed by a demon. Jesus goes around the villages. He sends out the disciples to preach, and speaks with them at length. John sends two of his disciples to him; John is praised. Christ reproaches the crowds concerning John. He reproaches the cities. He gives thanks to the Father. He calls those who are heavy-laden. He passes through the grainfields. He heals the man with the withered hand. And the Jews plot to kill him. When he withdraws from there, the crowd follows and is healed. So too the demon-possessed man who was blind and mute. Then the Jews say: "He casts out demons by Beelzebul." Then they ask for a sign; and he gave them the sign of Jonah. He foretold that the Ninevites would condemn them. Then he says [?]: "When the unclean spirit goes out, seeking rest." Then his mother seeks to speak with him. Getting into the boat, he tells the parable

of the sower, and the reason why he speaks in parables. He explains this parable and adds those of the treasure, the pearl, the field, the mustard seed, and the leaven. He explains the parable of the field in the house, and adds that of the net. He calls the disciples blessed, comparing them to a householder. He comes to his homeland, where the Jews take offence at him. Then he says: "A prophet is not without honour except in his own homeland." And hearing what had happened concerning Herod and John, he withdraws to a deserted place and feeds the five thousand. He sends the disciples off in the boat. He goes up the mountain to pray. He comes to them by night as they sail; he receives Peter on the waters. He comes to Gennesaret. Many are healed. The Pharisees complain about purifications; he silences them, and teaches the crowds about foods. Peter asks about what had been said, and Christ explains it more clearly. He came to Tyre, and the Canaanite woman approaches him. From there he goes to the mountain by the sea, and heals many. He feeds the four thousand men. He came to Magdala. The Jews ask for a sign. But he left them and went away to the other side. The disciples forgot to bring bread; he speaks to them about the leaven of the Pharisees. He goes out to Caesarea. He asks the disciples about himself; Peter confesses him. Then he foretells his passion, rebukes Peter, and commands whoever wishes to follow him to take up the cross. He also speaks of his second coming. He goes up the mountain, where he was also transfigured. As he comes down they ask him about Elijah, and they learn. The epileptic boy is brought to him and healed. He reproaches the disciples. In Galilee he speaks to them about his passion. In Capernaum those who collect the two-drachma tax come to him. The disciples ask who is the greatest. Then, calling a child, he says: "Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble," and, "If your eye or your hand causes you to stumble," and, "Do not despise one of these little ones." Then the parable of the hundred sheep, and, "If your brother sins against you, rebuke him," and, "If two of you agree, whatever they ask they will receive." Then Peter says: "How often shall my brother sin against me?" The parable of the man who owed ten thousand talents. He came into Judea. He healed many. He settled the question of divorce. He speaks about the kinds of eunuchs. He blesses the children. The rich man comes to him. The disciples ask, "Who can be saved?" Then he says: "You will sit on twelve thrones," and, "Whoever has left houses," and what follows. Then the parable of the labourers. And going up to Jerusalem, he told the disciples about his death. The wife of Zebedee makes a request on behalf of her sons concerning the first places. The apostles are indignant, and are taught. The two blind men of Jericho are healed. Then the

…the events concerning the donkey. He enters the temple, drives out those who were selling, and heals those who come to him. Then the children sing his praises. He goes out to Bethany, and on his way back to Jerusalem he withers the fig tree and says to the disciples, “Even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be thrown into the sea,’ it will happen; and whatever you ask in faith, you will receive.” The priests ask, “By what authority are you doing these things?” He asks them in return about the baptism of John. He tells them the parable of the two sons, then the parable of the vineyard and the wicked workers, then that of the wedding feast and the worthless guests. Then the Jews came to trap him in his speech, and there is the matter of the coin. The Sadducees ask about the woman who had been married to the seven brothers; then the lawyer asks, “Which commandment is the first?” Then Jesus asks them, “What do you think about the Christ?” When they had been silenced, he speaks to the crowds about the scribes and Pharisees, pronouncing woes on them. Then he goes up from the temple to the Mount of Olives and speaks to the disciples about what is to come. Then comes the parable of the servant put in charge of the household, and that of the ten virgins, and that of the five talents, and that of the goats and the sheep. The chief priests and the scribes gather to seize him. But he went to the house of Simon in Bethany, where the woman with the alabaster jar comes. Judas makes his bargain with the Jews. The disciples are sent to prepare the Passover. Christ exposes Judas. He hands down the mystery, where he says, “I will not drink of this fruit of the vine.” He goes out to the Mount of Olives. He foretells that the disciples will fall away. Leaving the disciples at Gethsemane and praying three times, he says, “Let us go from here.” Judas came with the crowd, and Peter cuts off the servant’s ear. They led Jesus to Caiaphas, tried him, condemned him, and mocked him. Peter denies him. They lead Jesus to Pilate. Judas hangs himself. Christ is tried. Pilate’s wife advises him to have nothing to do with Jesus. Then he is crucified. The women with Mary stood watching from a distance what was taking place. Joseph takes the body of the Lord. The Jews ask for the guard. The women with Mary came to the tomb in the evening, and there was an earthquake. They heard from the angel that he had risen. They are sent by Christ to the disciples. The Jews heard about the earthquake and the resurrection, and gave money to the guards so that they would lie. The eleven [?] came to Jesus in Galilee. He hands on to them the…

Book 2: the Gospel according to Mark. 15. John baptizes the Jews. Christ comes from Nazareth, was baptized, and went into the wilderness to be tempted. Then he goes into Galilee after John had been handed over, and calls Peter, James and their companions. He enters Capernaum and teaches,

[?] the demon-possessed man there, then Peter’s mother-in-law, and in the evening he heals many; he went out into the wilderness and went about Galilee. He heals the leper. He comes to Capernaum. He heals the paralytic; he teaches the crowd. He calls Levi the son of Alphaeus. He eats with the tax collectors. The Pharisees find fault with him over this. The disciples of John complain about fasting, and he answers them. He passes through the grainfields. He heals the man with the withered hand. He withdraws to the sea. A great multitude follows him. The demons confess him. He calls the twelve to him, in order to send them out. Then the Jews say, “He casts out the demons by Beelzebul.” His mother comes to him. He gets into the boat. He tells the parable of the sower, that of the field, and that of the mustard seed. The disciples are caught in a storm on the sea. Christ rebukes the sea. The demoniac in the country of the Gergesenes is healed. The pigs are drowned. He went across to the other side, and Jairus pleads on behalf of his daughter. Then the woman with the flow of blood is healed. He came to his home town, and they take offence at him. Here he says, “A prophet is not without honour except in his own home town.” He sends out the disciples two by two, giving them many instructions. Then the events concerning Herod and John. The disciples returned to him. He feeds the crowds. He comes to the disciples as they are caught in the storm. He came to Gennesaret and healed many. He speaks about unwashed hands. He came to Tyre. He heals the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman, then the deaf man with the speech impediment. He feeds the crowd. The Jews ask for a sign, and he does not give one. He speaks about the leaven of the Pharisees and rebukes the disciples. He heals the blind man at Bethsaida. He asks the disciples about himself. Peter confesses him, and is rebuked because of the passion. Here he says, “If anyone wants to come after me.” He is transfigured on the mountain and speaks about Elijah. A boy with epilepsy is brought to him and is healed. He foretells to the disciples his death and resurrection, and reproves them for having argued on the way about who was first. Here he says, “Whoever is not with me is against me,” concerning the man who was casting out demons in his name. Then he says, “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble,” and also, “Their worm will not die, nor is the fire quenched.” He speaks about divorce. He blesses the children. The rich man asks what he must do to live, and he answers him. Going up to Jerusalem, he speaks about the passion. The sons of Zebedee ask for the seats at his right hand. He speaks about humility. Bartimaeus receives his sight. Then the events concerning the colt; and he entered the temple, and when it was evening he went out to Bethany. Then comes the fig tree. He drives the sellers out of the temple. In the evening he went out of the city. Peter marvels at the fig tree. Jesus urges the disciples to believe. He commands them to forgive their neighbour’s sins. He returns to the city.

The Jews ask by what authority he does these things. He asks them about the baptism of John. He tells of the vineyard and the wicked tenants. Then about the tax, then about the seven brothers. The scribe asks which commandment is the first, and on learning the answer he accepts it. Christ asks about himself. Then he speaks against the Pharisees, and about the widow’s two coins. Going out of the temple, he speaks of its destruction. The disciples ask about the time, and he foretells many things to them. He came to Bethany, to Simon the leper. There the ointment is poured out. Judas makes his bargain with the Jews. The disciples are sent to prepare the Passover. He exposes Judas. He hands down the mysteries. He goes out to the Mount of Olives. He foretells to the disciples that they will fall away, and to Peter that he will deny him. He prays to the Father; then he is arrested. Peter cuts off the servant’s ear. The young man flees naked. Jesus is led to Caiaphas. They bear false witness against him. He confesses himself to be the Son of God. Peter denies him. Jesus is led to Pilate; he is crucified. There were there Mary the mother of James the younger, and the Magdalene, and Salome. Joseph takes the body of Jesus. The women came after the Sabbath, bringing spices. They saw the angel in the tomb and were afraid. Christ, having risen, appeared to Mary, from whom he had cast out the seven demons. She told the disciples, but they did not believe. After that he appeared to the two on the road, then to the eleven, and he reproached them for their unbelief. And he sent them out to preach, to baptize and to work signs. Then he was taken up. Book 3: according to Luke. 49. The events of the birth of John and of Christ; the events concerning Simeon. Anna gives thanks to the Lord. Jesus stays behind in the temple, and his parents did not know. John baptizes, and Christ too is baptized, being thirty years old. His genealogy is given. He is led into the wilderness. He comes to Nazareth; he reads in the synagogue. He spoke to the Jews about the widow in the time of Elijah and about Naaman the leper, and they wanted to throw him over a cliff. He came to Capernaum. He healed the demoniac, Peter’s mother-in-law and many others. He went out into the wilderness. He came to Gennesaret and got into Peter’s boat, where the net was also breaking. Simon was afraid. He healed the leper, then the paralytic. He calls Levi and eats at his house, and he is accused by the Pharisees over this, and because his disciples do not fast. On the second-first Sabbath he goes through the grainfields. On another Sabbath he heals the man with the withered hand. He chooses the twelve. He speaks the beatitudes. He pronounces woes on the rich and on those who laugh. He gives counsel about love, about not retaliating against one’s neighbour, and about kindness; about not judging, and about giving. He also tells a parable, the one about the tree, and about the one who keeps his words, that he is like the house on the rock. He comes to Capernaum. The centurion comes to him on behalf of his servant. Then the widow’s son

is raised. John sends his disciples to him. Jesus reproaches the crowd concerning John. He likens this generation to children calling out to one another. He comes into the house of a Pharisee, and behold, the sinful woman pours out the alabaster jar. The Pharisee finds fault with what has happened. Jesus tells him the parable of the two debtors. Then he went through city and village, and the women who had been healed followed him. He tells the parable of the sower. His mother came to him. The disciples sail with him, are caught in a storm, and come to Gadara, and the legion goes into the pigs. Then Jairus pleads on behalf of his daughter, and the woman with the flow of blood is healed. He raises the girl. He sends out the twelve disciples. Herod hears about him. Jesus withdraws to a deserted place. He feeds the crowds. He asks, “Who do people say that I am?” Peter confesses him. He orders them to keep silent. He foretells his passion and resurrection. He says, “If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself.” He is transfigured. He comes down from the mountain. He heals the boy with epilepsy. He speaks about the passion. The disciples were asking which of them would be the greatest, and Jesus taught them. Then he says, “Whoever is not against you is for you,” concerning the man who was casting out demons in his name but was not following him. When he wished to enter the city of the Samaritans, it did not receive him. Then the disciples wanted to call down fire on them, but Jesus rebuked them. Someone who wants to follow him is held back. Another is invited and draws back. Then he says, “No one puts his hand to the plough and turns back.” He appointed seventy disciples and sends them out two by two, instructing them to carry nothing. He reproaches the cities. Then he says, “Whoever hears you hears me.” Then he says, “I saw Satan fall like lightning,” and he gives the disciples authority over him, and urges them not to rejoice in this. Then he gives thanks to the Father, and says to the disciples, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For many prophets longed to see what you see.” The lawyer tests him, and the parable is told of the man going down to Jericho. Martha complains about her sister. He teaches the disciples to pray, and tells the parable of the man who asks for bread from his friend who is in bed. He heals the mute man who was possessed by a demon. Then they say, “He heals by Beelzebul.” Then he says, “When the unclean spirit goes out, it passes through waterless places.” Then a certain woman says, “Blessed is the womb,” and what follows. He foretells that the people of that time will be condemned by Nineveh, and says, “No one, after lighting a lamp, puts it under the bushel basket.” He went in to dine with a Pharisee. The Pharisee finds fault because he did not wash first. Then he says to him, “You clean the outside of the cup,” and he pronounces woes on them and on the lawyers. Then he says, “Nothing is hidden,”

and also, “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body,” and, “Are not five sparrows…,” and, “Whoever blasphemes against the Spirit.” Someone comes to him to have the inheritance divided with his brother. Then the rich man reasoning with himself about his barns. He urges them not to worry about food. He speaks about almsgiving, and about the master who serves his own servants, and about the faithful servant, and about the one who knows his master’s will and does not do it. And, “I came,” he says, “to cast fire.” He also spoke about those who interpret the appearance of the sky. And: “When you go with your opponent before a magistrate.” Then the Galileans killed by Pilate, and those who were buried under the tower. Then the parable of the barren fig tree. On the Sabbath he heals the woman bent over by the demon, and the Jews find fault, but he silences them. Then the parable of the mustard seed and of the leaven. Then he was asked whether those who are saved are few. He urges them to enter by the narrow door, and adds, “They will come from east and west and recline at table.” Then they say to him, “Get away, for Herod wants to kill you.” And he says, “Go and tell that fox.” Then he says to Jerusalem, “How often have I longed to gather your children together.” He heals the man with dropsy in the house of a Pharisee. He speaks about taking the place of honour, and about whom one ought to invite to a meal. Then the parable of the banquet and of those who declined to come. He urges them to disregard all their own family and follow him. Then the parable of the man building the tower and of the one preparing for war. Then he says, “Salt is good.” The Pharisees grumble because he welcomed tax collectors. He tells them parables: that of the lost sheep, that of the coin, and that of the prodigal son; about the steward who was dismissed; about love of money; about pride, and that everything in the law must be fulfilled; about the man who divorces his wife; about Lazarus and the rich man. About forgiving one’s neighbour’s sins. And, “Which of you,” he says, “who has a servant ploughing, does not give him orders when he comes in from the field?” Then the ten lepers. He foretells his coming. About praying always. He told the parable of the widow and of the unjust ruler. Then he says, “When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith?” The parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector. Then he calls the children to him. The rich man comes to him asking what he must do to inherit eternal life. He speaks to the disciples about the passion, but they did not understand. The blind man near Jericho is healed. The events concerning Zacchaeus. The parable of the man who wished to acquire a kingdom. The events concerning the colt. He foretells the capture of the city. He drives the sellers out of the temple. Then they say, “By what authority are you doing these things?” He asks them about the baptism

of John. Then the parable of the vineyard and the wicked tenants. The matters of the tax and of the woman married to the seven brothers. Then he asks them about himself: how they say that the Christ is the son of David; and he speaks about the best seats. The widow puts in two coins. He foretells the destruction of the temple and the evils to come. Judas makes his bargain with the Jews. He sends the disciples to prepare the Passover. Judas is exposed after the mystery. The disciples quarrel about who is first. Then he says to Simon, “Behold, Satan has demanded to have you,” and he foretells his denial, and tells the disciples to carry a purse. Then he is arrested. Peter denies him. Jesus is beaten by the Jews. He is asked whether he is the Christ, and he answers. He is led to Pilate and sent to Herod. Then he is led back to Pilate. He is handed over to be crucified; a crowd follows; he speaks to the women about the evils to come. He is crucified. Joseph buries the body. The women bring spices to the tomb and found no one.
