They learn from the two angels that he has risen. They report it to the disciples, but they did not believe. Peter ran to the tomb and found it so. Then he appears to the two travelling on the road. When they returned, they heard that he had appeared to Simon. Then he suddenly stood among them, and they were terrified. He showed them the marks, and ate in their presence. He led them out to Bethany and was taken up. Book 4: according to John. 50. John speaks of Christ as God. He speaks about the Baptist, then about Christ and the incarnation. The Baptist answers those who were sent to him. The next day he bears witness to Jesus, that the Spirit came down upon him. The next day he again bears witness to Jesus. And Andrew and his companion attach themselves to him. Andrew brings Peter to him. The next day Andrew calls Philip to him. The next day Jesus, having gone out into Galilee, calls Philip. He brings Nathanael to him. Jesus bears witness to him. The wedding takes place at Cana. Then he comes to Capernaum. He goes up to Jerusalem at the Passover; he drives out of the temple those who were selling doves. Many believe in him. Then the events concerning Nicodemus. Then he comes into Judea, and the disciples were baptizing

[?] …king, and he withdraws to the mountain. The disciples sailed to Capernaum. Jesus came there, and the crowds came too. Then he speaks to them about the mysteries. And, unable to bear the saying, they turned back. He says to the twelve, “Do you also want to go away?” Then Peter says, “You have the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go?” When it was the Feast of Tabernacles, his brothers urge him to go up to the temple. He went up later, and the Jews were looking for him, and were indignant because he had healed a blind man on the Sabbath. He speaks about the Paraclete; and some believed, while others did not believe. The officers are rebuked by the chief priests for not having arrested him. Nicodemus speaks to them, and they silence him. Again Jesus speaks to them, and they tried to overturn his words. Here comes the account of the woman accused of adultery. Again he says to them, “I am going where you cannot come.” And they supposed that he would kill himself. Then he foretells the manner of his death, and many believed in him. Then he says to them, “If you continue in my word, the truth will set you free,” and many other things. The Jews say to him, “You are a Samaritan and have a demon.” Again Jesus speaks to them at length, and among other things he added, “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” Then they wanted to stone him; but he went away from them and healed the blind man with mud. Then he speaks about the sheep and the shepherd who enters the fold through the door; and there was a division among the Jews. At the Feast of Dedication Jesus was walking in Solomon’s Portico. The Jews ask him whether he is the Christ. When he had spoken, they picked up stones to throw at him. When he asked them the reason, they came to seize him, and could not. He went away to where John had been baptizing. Martha and her sister send from Bethany on behalf of Lazarus. And when he wished to go into Judea, the disciples tried to stop him. He came to Bethany; he raised Lazarus. Again the Jews plotted to kill Jesus. Then Caiaphas prophesies. Jesus withdraws to the wilderness of Ephraim. Then the Jews were in doubt whether he would come to the feast. And six days before the Passover he came to Bethany. Then, as he was at dinner, Mary anointed him, and Judas is indignant. Jesus silences him. The Jews came to him there. Crowds with palm branches met him as he was coming into Jerusalem, riding on a young donkey. Then the Greeks seek to see him. Then he tells the parable of the grain of wheat, and speaks about those who fear death. Then he adds, “Father, glorify your Son,” and a voice came from heaven. The crowd thought it had thundered. Then he foretells to them the manner of his death and urges them to believe; but they would not believe, “so that,” it says, “the word of Isaiah might be fulfilled.” He washes the disciples’ feet; he exposes Judas, and Judas, having taken the morsel, went out into the night. Then Jesus speaks with the disciples. He gives them a commandment about love.

He foretells Peter’s denial. Philip asks to see the Father. He foretells to them the coming of the Paraclete; he speaks of many other things, and accuses the Jews. He foretells [?] to the disciples, then again things that are encouraging, and again things that are grievous. He speaks with the Father. Then he comes to the garden and is arrested. Peter cuts off the servant’s ear. They lead Jesus to Annas. The disciple brings Peter into the courtyard. The attendant strikes Jesus; he says to him, “If I have spoken wrongly,” and what follows. They send him to Caiaphas. Peter denies him. Jesus is led to Pilate. He is crucified, and they put up the inscription. There stood beside the cross his mother, and his mother’s sister Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Then he entrusts his mother to John. Joseph [?] the body. Nicode-

…of the apostles. And these are the names of the seven deacons: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus. Luke, then, recounts the acts of these apostles and deacons, and the signs done by them, which are these. Peter and John healed, in the name of the Lord, the man lame from birth who sat at the Beautiful Gate. Peter rebuked Ananias and Sapphira his wife, who had kept back part of the price of the field and of what they had promised to God, and they immediately fell dead. Peter, in Joppa, prayed and raised Dorcas from the dead after she had died. Peter saw the vessel let down from heaven, full of every kind of living creature. Peter's shadow, falling on the sick, healed them. Peter, while he was guarded and bound in prison, was set free by an angel without the soldiers knowing. And Herod was eaten by worms and breathed his last. Stephen did wonders and signs. Philip came upon the eunuch reading Isaiah, and baptized him. The same Philip drove out many spirits in Samaria, and the lame and paralysed were healed by him. Paul, as he drew near to Damascus, saw a vision and at once became an evangelist. Paul, in Lystra, healed Aeneas, who had been lame from birth, in the name of the Lord. Paul was called to Macedonia by a vision. Paul cleansed the woman who had a spirit of divination. Paul and Silas were thrown into prison at Philippi, and their feet were fastened in the stocks; but at midnight there was an earthquake, and their bonds were loosed. Handkerchiefs were carried from Paul's body to the sick and to those possessed by demons, and they were healed. Paul, at Troas, raised Eutychus, who had fallen from the window and died, saying: "His life is in him." Paul rebuked Elymas the magician, and he became blind. Paul, sailing to Rome, was caught in a storm, he and all who were on the ship, for fourteen days and nights. And when all expected to die, the Lord stood by him and said to him, "For your sake I have granted these men their lives," and they were saved. When Paul came out of the ship a viper bit him, and everyone thought he would die; but when he remained unharmed, they thought he was a god. Paul laid his hands on the father of Publius on the island, who was suffering from dysentery, and healed him, and he healed many others on the island who were sick. Book 6. The Catholic Epistles, seven; the first of these is that of James. 52. These too are named after those who wrote them. James himself writes this one to those of the twelve tribes who are scattered abroad and have believed in our Lord Jesus Christ. He writes the Epistle as a work of teaching, instructing them about the different kinds of temptation, which comes from God and which from people's own hearts; and that faith must be shown not

in word alone but also in deed; and that it is not the hearers of the law but the doers who are justified. He also gives instructions about the rich: that in the churches the rich should not be preferred to the poor, but rather should be rebuked as proud. And finally, having comforted those who suffer wrong and urged them to be patient until the coming of the Judge, and having taught about endurance from the example of Job [?], he instructs them to call the elders to the sick, and to be eager to turn back to the truth those who have gone astray, for the reward of this from the Lord is the forgiveness of sins. And so he completes the Epistle. Second, that of Peter. 53. This one too bears the name of its writer. Peter himself writes this Epistle as a work of teaching to the Jews in the dispersion who have become Christians. Since they came to faith from among the Jews, he strengthens them. And first he explains and demonstrates that faith in Christ was announced by the prophets, and that through them the redemption by his blood was made known; and that all these things, into which angels long to look, have been proclaimed as good news both to them and to the Gentiles. Then, having counselled them to live worthily of the one who called them, he also urges them to honour the king, and commands wives and husbands to be of one mind. And after giving a few exhortations concerning conduct, he indicates that the Lord's preaching of salvation and resurrection reached even into Hades, so that the dead too might rise, and be judged in the body, yet abide by the grace of the resurrection; and that the end of all things has now drawn near, and all must be ready, as those who will give account to the Judge. And so he completes the Epistle. Third, again that of Peter. 54. Likewise this one, being written by the same man, bears his name. Peter himself sends this one too to those who have already believed. The Epistle is a reminder of the first. For knowing that his departure from the body would be soon, he was eager to remind everyone of the teaching in which they had been instructed. And first he explains about faith and shows that it was proclaimed by the prophets, and that the prophecies about the Saviour are not human but were spoken by God. Next he instructs them not to pay heed to deceivers, saying that their destruction will come, just as it came upon the angels who transgressed. In the Epistle he also foretells that there will be days in which scoffers will go about and seek to deceive some, saying that the coming of the Saviour is proclaimed by us in vain, since it is always spoken of and has never yet happened. He instructs them to keep away above all from such people, teaching them not to grow slack over the passing of time. For all time is nothing before the Lord, since one day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day. But he affirms

that the day of the Lord will come quickly, and demonstrates it, and commands everyone to be ready for it in good works, and to love what was written by the apostle Paul, and not to pay heed to those who slander it, since such people slander all the divine Scriptures as well. Having thus reminded and taught everyone to know things beforehand, he exhorts them not to fall away from the goal of faith, and so he completes the Epistle. Fourth, that of John. 55. This one too is so called because John the evangelist himself sends it, reminding those who have already believed in the Lord. And first, as in the Gospel, so in this Epistle he speaks of the divinity of the Word, demonstrating that he is eternally in God, and teaching that the Father is light, so that in this way we may know that the Word is the radiance from him. In speaking of God, he explains that the mystery that concerns us is not something new, but that it has always existed from the beginning, and has now been made manifest in the Lord, who is eternal life and true God. He also sets out the reason for the Word's coming and appearing, saying that it was to destroy the works of the devil, so that we might be freed from death and might know the Father and the Son himself, our Lord Jesus Christ. So he writes to every age, to little children, to young men, to old men, that God has been made known, and that the devil's working has now been defeated, since death has been abolished. Then throughout the rest of the Epistle he teaches about love, wishing us to love one another, since Christ also loved us. So he explains the difference between fear and love, between the children of God and the children of the devil, about sin that leads to death and sin that does not, and about the difference between spirits. And so he distinguishes which spirit is from God and which is of error, and when we are known to be children of God and when children of the devil; and for what kind of sin we ought to pray; and that whoever does not love his neighbour is not worthy of his calling, nor can he be said to be Christ's. He also shows the unity of the Son with the Father, and that whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either. In this Epistle he also gives a distinguishing mark, stating what is peculiar to the Antichrist: namely, to say that Jesus is not himself the Christ, so that, as if he did not exist, the liar may say that he himself is. Throughout the Epistle he exhorts those who believe in the Lord not to lose heart if they are hated in the world, but rather to rejoice, because the world's hatred shows that believers have passed out of the world itself and now belong to the heavenly commonwealth. And at the end of the Epistle he reminds them again, saying that the Son of God is eternal life and true God, and that we should serve him and keep ourselves from idols. Fifth, again that of John. 56. This one he writes as the elder to a lady and to her

children. The occasion of the Epistle is this: seeing that her children were living well in the faith, and that many deceivers were going about saying that Christ's coming was not in the flesh, he writes the Epistle. And first he commends her children for walking rightly; then, teaching that the mystery that concerns us is not new, he again exhorts them about love, and that they should remain in the teaching handed down to them. And then he teaches that whoever says that Christ has not come in the flesh is an antichrist. He instructs that no one should receive such people into the house or even greet them, and so he completes the Epistle. Sixth, again that of John. 57. This one too is John's, as its title states. It is addressed to Gaius. And first he commends him, as one to whom all bear witness for his hospitality, and urges him to continue in the same purpose, and to send the brothers on their way and welcome them. Again he commends his purpose, but he blames Diotrephes, since he not only gives nothing himself to the poor but also hinders others, and talks much nonsense. Such people, he says, are strangers to the truth and do not even know God. But he commends Demetrius, bearing him the best of testimony. Seventh, that of Jude. 58. Jude writes this Epistle, as its title states, to those who have already believed. The occasion is this: since certain people had slipped in, teaching that sin is a matter of indifference and denying the Lord, he felt compelled to write and to secure the brothers. And first he urges them to contend for and remain in the faith handed down to them; then he denounces such people as deceivers, and instructs them to have no fellowship at all with such people, knowing that it is not enough merely to be called unless we also walk worthily of the calling. For the Lord, having brought the former people out of Egypt, destroyed them when they did not remain in the faith [?]; and he did not spare the angels who did not keep their own rank. One must therefore withdraw from such people. For even Michael the archangel did not bring a slanderous charge against the devil. And so he teaches that their destruction will be like that of Sodom. Then he gives exhortations about conduct, and having prayed for them to receive steadfastness in the faith from the Lord, he completes the Epistle.

Book 7. The Epistles of Paul, fourteen. The first of these is that to the Romans. 59. They are so called because Paul himself sends them personally; and through them he reminds and corrects those whom he had already seen and taught, while those whom he had not seen he is eager to instruct and teach, as one can learn from those who read them. This one to the Romans he sends from Corinth, not yet having seen the Romans, but having heard about them and longing to see them. And first he commends their faith, which is proclaimed

everywhere [?]; then he indicates that he had often intended to come because of his longing for them, but had not yet been able to. And then he makes the Epistle a work of teaching about the calling of the Gentiles: that circumcision was for a time and has now ceased; that through Christ the transgression of Adam has been undone; and that the shadow of the law has passed away. He establishes that the calling of the Gentiles came about in due order in this way: he demonstrates that the law is innate in all people, and that all, by untaught nature and from creation itself, are able to know God. That is why he rightly blames the Greeks first, since God had revealed to them, from the works of the world, the knowledge of himself and of his eternal power, which is his Word, in whom and through whom he made all things; yet they did not rather recognize from the creatures that their maker is God, but on the contrary made gods of the works themselves, and worshipped the creation rather than the Creator. He also blames the Jews, since they did not keep the law, and rather dishonoured God by transgressing the law. And so he convicts both parties, Jews and Greeks alike, and shuts them up together under lawlessness, to show that, all having become equal, as equally liable, they also need the Redeemer. And since grace and redemption have come equally to the Jews and to the Gentiles, the calling of the Gentiles has rightly come about; and since the calling of the Gentiles has come about, circumcision and the shadow in the law have necessarily ceased. For Abraham, he says, was justified not in circumcision but before circumcision, and was renamed Abraham because he was to be the father of many nations, according to the faith he had while uncircumcised; and after being justified he received circumcision in the flesh as well, so that it might be a sign to those born of him according to the flesh that circumcision would cease when the nations became children of Abraham, having begun to live according to the faith of Abraham, by which he was justified when he was uncircumcised. It was for these reasons that he was renamed from Abram to Abraham. And when the things signified have come, the sign must cease. If, then, they compel the Gentiles to be circumcised, let them do away with the name Abraham too, and let him be called Abram; but if he was renamed Abraham by God, the Gentiles must not be circumcised, nor indeed the Jews according to the flesh any longer, so that the name may stand firm and he may be called the father of many nations. For no one any longer needs to be circumcised, being content with the faith of Abraham; nor does he need the rest of the shadow in the law. For one is justified not by these things but by faith, just as Abraham was. Having established these points, he demonstrates further that redemption and grace could not otherwise come to Israel and to the Gentiles unless the ancient sin, which through Adam came upon all, were undone. And he says that this could not be wiped out by anyone other than the Son, through whom the creation had also come about in the beginning. For it was not possible for another to undo the transgression. Then he writes that this could not otherwise come about

unless the Son of God, taking a body, became a man, so that, offering this body (I mean the body subject to the same sufferings as ours) on behalf of all, he might free all from death; and that, just as through one man sin entered the world, so also through one man grace might come to all people. And then, like a good steward, he consoles the Jews: "You do not become transgressors of the law if you believe in Christ"; while he charges those from the Gentiles not to exalt themselves against Israel, but to know that they have been grafted onto them as branches onto the root. After this, having given words of exhortation about conduct, he completes the

Second, to the Corinthians. 60. The same Paul sends this one to the Corinthians from Ephesus in Asia, having already seen and taught them, but nevertheless reminding them through this Epistle. The occasion of the Epistle is this: the Corinthians, gathering together in a spirit of rivalry, were divided in their opinions, and so there were divisions among them; and because there were divisions, they overlooked the man who had taken his stepmother as his wife. Others wanted to leave their wives on the pretext of self-restraint. Some were even eating in idol temples, as though food sacrificed to idols were a matter of indifference. Others despised everyone else but admired those who spoke in tongues. And finally they had been deceived even about the mystery of the resurrection, saying that this flesh is not raised. Since all these things were stirring in Corinth, the people write to the Apostle, and he replies on every point. And first he bears witness to their understanding and knowledge; but he does not approve of them for causing divisions, and advises them to regard virtue as lying not in word but in deed and power. Then, having rebuked the man who had taken his stepmother, and having exhorted them not to have lawsuits against one another, he goes on to answer what they had written about. On marriage he teaches that the union is indissoluble, and that they should abstain only for a season for the sake of prayer; and because they loved self-restraint, he writes about virginity, that it should come about not by compulsion but by persuasion. Then about food sacrificed to idols: that they should not misuse their knowledge but live by love. So he forbids banquets in idol temples, so that the little ones may not be made to stumble. Then he writes about spiritual gifts: that they should not quarrel over the gifts, nor prefer the one who has this gift to the one who has that, for he says all are from the same Spirit. And then he teaches about the resurrection: that the flesh is raised, dying perishable but rising imperishable, by the grace of Christ. He establishes the resurrection from the fact that Christ has been raised. And at the end he writes words of exhortation about conduct, gives instructions about the collection for the saints, and so completes the Epistle.

Third, again to the Corinthians. 61. He sends this one too to the same people, from Macedonia. The occasion of the Epistle is this: when the Corinthians received the earlier Epistle, they were pierced with remorse over the sin of the man who had taken his stepmother, and were grieved at having overlooked such a sin. But then they were being carried away by certain people, the very ones who were also giving occasion for the divisions, so as to cling to the letter of the law and regard the grace of Christ as a matter of indifference; and they paid more heed to those who boasted in outward appearance. Yet they were also attending well to the collection for the saints. So the Apostle replies to these matters. And first he commends them for having expelled the transgressor; then, at their request, he consents and orders that the man, having repented, be received back. In this Epistle he teaches about the law, analysing the letter, and shows that one must not take only the letter of the law, but search out the meaning within the letter itself; for the law is not merely its words, but within the words is also the mind of the Spirit. Next he shows that since Christ has come there is a new creation, and one must not live according to the old, but be renewed in all things as in a new creation, and that circumcision is now of no effect. He commends them also for their ministry, and urges them to abound in it still more. Then, blaming those who boasted in outward appearance, he lists everything he has suffered for the Lord's sake, and he recounts the visions he saw when he was caught up into Paradise and into the third heaven. Then, having instructed them not to sin, and those who sin to repent, he completes the Epistle with thanksgiving. Fourth, to the Galatians. 62. He sends this one from Rome, having already seen and taught them. The occasion of the Epistle is this: the Galatians, having been well taught by the Apostle and having sincerely believed in Christ, were, after he had gone away, carried away by certain people so as to be circumcised. Learning of this, the Apostle writes to them. And first, while bearing witness to the faith they had and to their sincere disposition in Christ, he reproaches them for having acted foolishly and for having changed course. Then he discusses the law and faith after the pattern of Abraham; and he demonstrates, both from the law and from Abraham's wives, which he interprets allegorically, that the shadow and circumcision were given until a set time, and that they are now made void by the coming of Christ. And having so demonstrated, he instructs them to pay no more heed to those who deceived them, but rather to hold fast to faith in Christ, and to know that the grace in Christ abolishes circumcision according to the flesh. And so, having again exhorted and taught them about conduct, he completes the Epistle. Fifth, to the Ephesians. 63. He sends this one from Rome, not yet having seen them but having heard about them. The occasion…

…The occasion of the Epistle is this. The Ephesians had believed in our Lord Jesus Christ and held a genuine faith in him and love for all the saints, and they wished to be strengthened by Paul. When the Apostle learned of this, he wrote them this Epistle as a kind of instruction in the faith. First he shows that the mystery that concerns us is nothing new, but that from the beginning, from the foundation of the world, it was God's good pleasure that Christ should suffer for us and that we should be saved. Next he discusses the calling of the Gentiles, to show that they were right to believe. He demonstrates that our calling came about not through a man but through Christ, who is the Son of God, so that from this too they might learn that in believing in Christ they had not become worshippers of a man, but true worshippers of God. He also indicates that he himself was sent for this purpose, to preach the Gospel, and that he cared for them. Then in the Epistle he sets out words of exhortation for husbands and wives, fathers and children, masters and slaves, and in general he prepares everyone against the devil and his demons, saying that our wrestling is against them. And like a good trainer who has anointed everyone with his words against the workings of the devil, he thus brings the Epistle to a close. Sixth [?], to the Philippians. 64. He sends this one from Rome, having seen them and taught them. The occasion of the Epistle is this. The Philippians had sent Paul a gift for his needs, and certain people were going about and corrupting the ears of the simple on the pretext of the shadow of the law and of circumcision, saying that without it one could not be justified. When the Apostle learned of this, he wrote to the Philippians. First he commends their faith and indicates that he remembers them. Then he relates how he made his defense in Rome, and that some had become a burden to him in his chains, stirring up envy against him. Then he urges them to love one another, explaining the Savior's love for humankind: that, being God, he became man for our sake. Then, taking up the subject of circumcision and the old law, he shows that circumcision has henceforth been rendered void, taking himself as the example and saying, "I count all these things loss because of Christ." Therefore he rebukes those who still teach circumcision and wish to deceive them, and says that they are enemies of Christ. But he commends the Philippians for the gift they shared with him, and after exhorting them once more concerning their conduct, he brings the Epistle to a close. Seventh, to the Colossians. 65. He sends this one from Rome, not having seen them, but having heard about them. The occasion of the Epistle is this. Certain people were trying to deceive the Colossians with Greek sophistries against faith in Christ, and concerning the foods in the law and circumcision. So when

the Apostle learned of these things, he wrote them this Epistle as a kind of instruction in the faith. First, giving thanks to God, he indicates that they have passed from darkness into the light of truth, and that Christ, in whom they believed, is the image of God and the Word through whom all things came to be; and that it was fitting that he, being the Creator, should become both the firstborn of creation and the firstborn from the dead, so that he might join the two together and give life to all things. He urges them to remain in the faith, indicating that Paul himself is a minister of the Gospel in which they were instructed. Then he takes up the law and the foods in it, and days and years, which he explains, and he shows that all the old things, and circumcision, have henceforth been rendered void. He advises them not to be led astray by those who use sophistries and wish to lead them astray. And finally, after exhorting here too parents and children, husbands and wives, slaves and masters, and giving the rest of his counsel concerning conduct, he brings the Epistle to a close. He instructs them, however, that when the Epistle has been read among them, they should have it read in the church of the Laodiceans as well, and that they in turn should read the one from Laodicea. Eighth, to the Thessalonians. 66. He sends this one from Athens, having seen them earlier and stayed among them. The occasion of the Epistle is this. The Apostle had suffered many afflictions in Beroea, in Philippi of Macedonia, and in Corinth, and knowing all he had suffered in Thessalonica too, he was afraid that the Thessalonians, hearing what he had suffered in the cities just mentioned, might be tempted by the tempter and be made to stumble. And learning also that they were grieving over those who were dying, he sent Timothy to them with this Epistle. First he strengthens them in the faith, so that they will not be shaken by the afflictions; for he reminds them that even in their instruction in the faith they were taught to endure afflictions, and that they had suffered nothing strange at the hands of the Jews, who also killed Christ. For he said that it is the lot of Christians to be afflicted in this life. After exhorting them at length to live as they had received from him, he writes also about those who have died, consoling them and teaching them not to take it hard; for death, he says, is not destruction but the road to resurrection. Then he teaches them about the times as well, so that, knowing the day to be uncertain, they may always be ready and pay no attention to anyone who makes claims about it. For he says that the coming will be such that those who are left and are found alive on that day will not precede those raised from the dead; for he teaches that the change of all will happen at once. In addition, urging them to improve in their conduct, he exhorts them always to rejoice in hope, to pray, and to give thanks to the Lord always, adjuring them to read this Epistle to all the brothers; and so he brings it to a close.

Ninth, this one too to the Thessalonians. 67. He sends this one from Rome. The occasion of the Epistle is this. Certain idle and disorderly people in Thessalonica were going about and unsettling the brothers, as though the coming of the Lord were already at hand. They deceived their hearers by claiming that the Apostle was making this known, and that they had heard it by the Spirit. When the Apostle learned of this, he wrote the Epistle. First he commends their growing faith, and says that he boasted of them because they were nobly enduring afflictions for Christ's sake; and he consoles them with the assurance that there will be vengeance from God against those who do wrong. Then he teaches about the coming of the Savior, telling them not to be persuaded by anyone or alarmed, whether by a spirit or as though by a letter from him, and not to think at all that it is already present; nor will it come until the apostasy comes first, and after it the Antichrist, the son of destruction, whose coming, he indicates, will be with lying signs and wonders by the working of Satan. Then, after exhorting them to stand firm nobly and to hold fast to the traditions as they were taught by him, he instructs them to have no fellowship with the disorderly, but even to cast them out; for he made it plain that such people are busybodies and deceivers. And in general he instructed that anyone who does not obey his words should be put out of the congregation. And finally, after praying for peace for them, he brings the Epistle to a close, writing the greeting with his own hand, which he declared to be the sign of every genuine letter of his. Tenth, to the Hebrews. 68. He sends this one from Italy. The occasion of the Epistle is this. Since the Jews were holding fast to the law and its shadows, the apostle Paul, who had become the teacher of the Gentiles and had been sent to the Gentiles to preach the Gospel, and had written to all the Gentiles, finally writes also to all the Hebrews from the circumcision who had believed this Epistle of demonstration concerning the coming of Christ and the cessation of the shadow of the law. First he shows that the prophets were sent for this purpose, to announce the Savior, and that after them he himself would come; that the prophets were servants and heralds of his coming, while Christ himself is the Son of God, through whom all things came to be; and that this Son had to become man, taking flesh, so that through the sacrifice of his body he might abolish death; for salvation would come to human beings not through the blood of a calf or a goat, but through the blood of Christ. He shows that the law made no one perfect but had a shadow of the good things to come, and that the people did not enter into rest, but the day of rest remains for all of us in common. Again he shows that the high-priestly ministry was transferred from Aaron to Christ, of whom Melchizedek was a type, not being of the tribe of Levi; and that the fathers were justified by faith

Eleventh, to Timothy. 69. He sends this one from Macedonia. The occasion of the Epistle is this. In Ephesus certain Judaizers were attempting to teach a different doctrine and to deceive the simple on the pretext of the law. When the Apostle learned of this, he urged Timothy to remain there to correct them, and he wrote him this Epistle. First he reminds him, as one who knows the faith in Christ, teaching him about the law, to restrain those who speak contrary to sound teaching and to rebuke them. For he himself had handed over to Satan Hymenaeus and Alexander, who had made shipwreck of the faith, so that they might be taught not to blaspheme. Having reminded him of these things, he then lays down for him church rules: about prayer—how, where, and for whom one ought to pray; about women keeping silent in the churches, and learning rather than teaching; about the appointment of bishops, presbyters, and deacons—how they should be appointed and what sort of people they must be; about the widows in the Church—from what age they should be enrolled, what sort of women they must be, and how they should be cared for; about the younger women being self-controlled, and marrying rather than living shamefully; and about charging the rich not to be haughty or to set their hope on wealth. Having given instructions on these matters, he urges him to teach these things, and no longer to drink only water, but to pay attention to himself and to his teaching, knowing that there will be times in which some will fall away from the faith. And after teaching that foods too are clean, and instructing him to avoid contentious questions as [?], in which some, boasting of them, have transgressed the faith, he brings the Epistle to a close. Twelfth, this one too to Timothy. 70. He sends this one again to Timothy, from Rome. The occasion of this Epistle too is as follows. Since those who had traveled with Paul had deserted him, the Apostle, wishing Timothy to come to him, writes the Epistle. First he makes clear that he remembers Timothy's devotion and the faith of his forebears; then, that those from Asia, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes, turned away from him when they saw his chains. But he commends Onesiphorus, who came to Rome and stayed with him. He instructs Timothy to avoid foolish questions, because quarrels arise from them; for Hymenaeus and Philetus, having been turned aside in this way, transgressed the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they are overturning the faith of some. Rather, then, he exhorts him to pay attention to himself and to his teaching, and to know that in the last times people will be lovers of pleasure

rather than lovers of God, and, foreseeing these things, to safeguard the people, so that none of them may be deceived. After urging him at length concerning conduct and exactness in teaching, and indicating that the time of his own departure has now arrived and that he is about to be poured out as an offering and to bear witness as a martyr, he charged him to come to him quickly, bringing the cloak and the books. He also warned him to beware of Alexander the coppersmith, who had done him much harm. And so he brings the Epistle to a close. Thirteenth, to Titus. 71. He sends this one from Nicopolis, for he spent the winter there. The occasion of the Epistle is this. He had left Titus in Crete to appoint clergy city by city; and since there were many there who were attempting to deceive the people on the pretext of the law, when the Apostle learned of it he wrote. First, giving thanks to God for Titus's devotion, he indicates that the faith in Christ is nothing new, but was prepared from eternity and promised by God. Then he deals with the appointment of the clergy, and teaches him how they should be appointed and what sort of people they must be. He commands him to rebuke those who contradict the sound faith, especially those of the circumcision, and to know that the Cretans are idle and need rebuking. After teaching that all foods are clean to the clean, and what sort of women the older women must be, since they ought to train the young women in self-control, he exhorts that slaves should be subject to their own masters. And finally, after reminding him that the Savior's grace justified us not by works but by his own love for humankind, and instructing him to avoid quarrels about the law as shameful, he tells him to come to him after he has sent Artemas to him. He also charged him to teach, and to have his own people devote themselves to good works. And so he brings the Epistle to a close. Fourteenth, to Philemon. 72. He sends this one from Rome. The occasion of the Epistle is this. Onesimus, Philemon's household slave, ran away, came to Paul, was instructed in the faith by him, and became useful to him for service. So he writes to Philemon about him, commending Onesimus to him, so that he may care for him sincerely and no longer treat him as a slave but as a brother. He also urged him to prepare lodging for him, so that if he comes he may find somewhere to stay. And so he brings the Epistle to a close. Book 8. The Revelation of John. 73. The book is so called because John himself, the evangelist and theologian, saw this revelation on the island called Patmos, on the Lord's Day, and at a command wrote it down to send to these seven churches: to Ephesus, to Smyrna, to Pergamum, to Thyatira, to Sardis, to Philadelphia, and to Laodicea. The things in the vision are many and varied. At the end he saw the destruction of the Antichrist together with the devil. He is commanded first to write to each

angel of the churches just mentioned according to the deeds of each. He saw many marvelous visions. He saw seven golden lampstands, and in their midst one like a Son of Man; and it was explained to him that the lampstands are the seven churches, and the one in their midst is the Lord. He also saw a door opened in heaven, and the Lord seated on a throne, and twenty-four elders seated on thrones and worshipping the Lord. He saw seals being opened, and as each was opened a vision took place. Then he saw seven angels holding seven trumpets, and as each blew his trumpet a sign took place; and when the seventh blew his trumpet, he heard voices saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the Lord's." And he saw the ark of the covenant in heaven. Then he saw a woman in labor, and a dragon of fire pursuing her. The woman was saved in the wilderness, but the dragon was thrown into the fire. Then he saw a beast with ten horns and seven heads, and its diadem full of blasphemy. He did not reveal its name, but the number of its name: 666. He also heard virgins singing and following the Lamb; and he saw an angel flying in midheaven, and another following, and another; and a white cloud, and seated on it one like a Son of Man, with a golden crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand. Then he saw seven angels holding the seven last plagues, and golden bowls full of the wrath of God. Then he was carried away in the spirit into a wilderness, and he saw a woman seated on a scarlet beast that had seven heads; and he indicated that the Antichrist would come from her. Then he saw heaven opened, and a white horse with its rider, and his name was called the Word of God. Then he saw the beast and the kings of the earth wishing to make war with the one seated on the white horse. And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophet, who was the Antichrist, and he saw them thrown into the lake of fire. Then he saw an angel coming down from heaven and throwing Satan and those who bore his mark into the abyss, and shutting it over him, so that he might no longer lead the nations astray until a thousand years had passed. Then he saw the martyrs reigning in glory in Christ. Then he saw that after a thousand years Satan will be released, and will be thrown into the lake of fire with the Antichrist for ever and ever. Then he saw a new heaven and a new earth, and the new Jerusalem; and he saw a river of the water of life, and the servants of God beholding his face and bearing his name on their foreheads. Having seen these things, John fell down, wishing to worship the angel who was showing him all these things. But the angel stopped him, saying, "Do not worship me, but God; for I am your fellow servant." And as he saw these things, he heard from our Lord
Jesus Christ that he who is, is, and that he is the Word of God, who later took flesh for our sake—I mean, became perfect man—and was called Son

There are also various other books besides those mentioned above, belonging to each Testament, that is, the Old and the New: some disputed, others apocryphal. The disputed books of the Old Testament we have already listed earlier: the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, Esther, Judith, and Tobit. Along with these the following are also counted: four books of Maccabees, the Ptolemaica, the Psalms and Ode of Solomon, and Susanna. These are the disputed books of the Old Testament. The apocrypha of the Old Testament [?]

74. Enoch, the Patriarchs, the Prayer of Joseph, the Testament of Moses, the Assumption of Moses, Abraham, Eldad and Modad, Elijah the prophet, Zephaniah the prophet, Zechariah the father of John, and the pseudepigrapha of Baruch, Habakkuk, Ezekiel, and Daniel. And again, these are the disputed books of the New Testament: 76. The Circuits of Peter, the Circuits of John, the Circuits of Thomas, the Gospel according to Thomas, the Teaching of the Apostles, and the Clementines, from which the truer and divinely inspired portions were selected and paraphrased. These are the books that are read. All these have been set out only for the sake of information, but they are entirely spurious and illegitimate, and to be rejected. None of them, especially the apocrypha, is approved or profitable—above all those of the New Testament. Rather, all of them, apart from those discussed above and approved by the wise men and fathers of old, truly deserve to be hidden away rather than read. This applies to everything else, and especially to the so-called Gospels among them, other than these four that have been handed down to us. For the holy canons of the holy, catholic, and apostolic Church have laid down four Gospels for us: that according to Matthew, that according to Mark, that according to Luke, and that according to John, in accordance with the prophecy of the vision that Ezekiel the prophet saw concerning the four cherubim. For this prophet saw four cherubim: the first like a man, that is, the Gospel according to Matthew; the second like a calf, that is, the Gospel according to Mark; another like a lion, that is, the Gospel according to Luke; and the fourth like an eagle, that is, the Gospel according to John. Besides these four there is no other Gospel. Now the Gospel according to Matthew was written by Matthew himself in the Hebrew language and published in Jerusalem, and it was translated by James, the brother of the Lord according to the flesh, who also first

[?] …who was ordained bishop by the holy apostles in Jerusalem. The Gospel according to Mark was dictated by the apostle Peter in Rome, and published by the blessed apostle Mark, who preached it in Alexandria, in Egypt, in the Pentapolis and in Libya. The Gospel according to Luke was dictated by the apostle Paul, and composed and published by the blessed Luke, apostle and physician; just as the apostle Peter likewise dictated the Acts of the Apostles, and the same man wrote them down

The Gospel according to John was dictated by the holy John himself, the apostle and beloved disciple, while he was in exile on the island of Patmos, and it was published by him in Ephesus through Gaius, the beloved host of the apostles, of whom Paul also speaks when writing to the Romans: "Gaius, my host and the host of the whole church, greets you." What and how many editions of the divine Scripture there are, that is, translations from Hebrew into Greek, who made them, and when. [?] The first is that of the Seventy-two translators. These were Hebrews, six chosen from each tribe, and they translated the divine Scripture under King Ptolemy Philadelphus, two hundred and thirty years before the birth in the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ. The second is that of Aquila. He came from Sinope in Pontus and, being a Greek, was baptized in Jerusalem. Then he rejected Christianity, went over to the Jews, and translated the divine Scripture with a perverse intent under the emperor Hadrian, who was stricken with leprosy, three hundred and thirty years after the translation of the Seventy-two. The third translation is that of Symmachus. He was a Samaritan, and because he was not honored by his own people, being sick with love of power, he went over to the Jews

and was circumcised a second time. He too translated the divine Scripture, to subvert the Samaritans, under the emperor Severus, fifty-six years after Aquila's translation. The fourth is that of Theodotion of Ephesus. He belonged to the heresy of Marcion of Pontus, but, angry with the members of his heresy, he too made a translation under the emperor Commodus, at that same time, to overturn his own heresy. The fifth translation is the one found hidden in jars at Jericho under the emperor Antoninus Caracalla by one of the scholars in Jerusalem.
